SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Perpendiculars and copying line segments (B7.3.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Perpendicular lines are lines that meet at right angles (90°). [1 mark]
(b) Draw a ray from R [1]; open the compasses to the length PQ (6 cm) [1]; with R as centre, draw an arc to cut the ray; the cut-off segment is the copy of PQ [1]. (Follows the curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.1 E.g.1.)
(c) (i) Erect a perpendicular at M: with M as centre, cut off equal arcs on both sides of M on the line [1]; from each of these points, draw arcs of equal radius to cross above (or below) the line [1]; join M to the crossing point to obtain the perpendicular [1]. (ii) Drop a perpendicular from P: with P as centre, draw an arc cutting the line at two points [1]; from each of these points, draw equal arcs that cross on the far side of the line [1]; join P to the crossing point [1]. (Follows the curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.1 E.g.2.)
Question 2 — Perpendicular bisectors (B7.3.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) A line that cuts a line segment into two equal parts at right angles (i.e. passes through the midpoint at 90°). [2 marks: 1 for “two equal parts / midpoint”, 1 for “at right angles”.]
(b) Correct construction with clear arcs from both end points [3 marks]; each half = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm [1]. (Curriculum exemplar: draw and bisect AB = 8 cm.)
(c) Correct construction [3 marks]; each half = 5.5 ÷ 2 = 2.75 cm [1]. (Curriculum exemplar: draw and bisect AB = 5.5 cm.)
Question 3 — Copying and bisecting angles (B7.3.1.2.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Draw a line and locate a point B on it [1]; with the vertex of the given angle as centre, draw an arc cutting both arms; with the same radius and B as centre, draw an arc on the new line [1]; transfer the chord between the arc and arms onto the new arc, then join B to the mark to obtain the copied angle [1]. (Follows the curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.3 E.g.1.)
(b) Neat acute angle drawn and labelled ∠ABC [1]; correct bisection with arcs [2]; the two angles measured are equal (within ±2° of half the original) [1].
(c) 120° ÷ 2 = 60° [1]; 60° ÷ 2 = 30° [1]; the smallest angle is 30° [1].
Question 4 — Constructing 90°, 45°, 60° and 30° (B7.3.1.2.4–.5)  [10 marks]
(a) Erect a perpendicular at the point (raising a right angle) [2]; verified with a protractor reading 90° (±2°) [1]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.4 E.g.1.)
(b) Correct bisection of the 90° angle giving 45° [2]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.4 E.g.2.)
(c) Correct 60° construction (equilateral-triangle method) with clear arcs [3]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.5 E.g.1.)
(d) Correct bisection giving 30° [2]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.5 E.g.2.)
Question 5 — Constructing 15° and 75° (B7.3.1.2.6)  [10 marks]
(a) Construct 60° [1]; bisect it to obtain 30° [1]; bisect 30° to obtain 15° [1]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.6 E.g.1.)
(b) Construct a right angle (90°) at the point [1]; obtain the 60° position by the usual arc [1]; bisect the arc between 60° and 90° [1]; join through the point to obtain 75°, verified within ±2° [1]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.6 E.g.3.)
(c) Construction of 75° [2]; each bisected angle = 75° ÷ 2 = 37.5° [1]. (Curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.2.6 E.g.4.)
Question 6 — Constructions in the environment (B7.3.1.2.7)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) Any two valid examples, e.g. the corner of a wall/floor, a window or door frame, the edges of a box or blackboard [2 marks]; (ii) any two valid examples, e.g. the central member of a symmetric roof frame, the crease of a folded paper corner, a symmetric kite design [2 marks]. (Follows curriculum exemplar E.g.1: buildings, water tanks, boxes.)
(b) 90° [1]; a right angle [1].
(c) He constructs/verifies a 90° angle between the wall and the floor (e.g. using a right-angle guide or plumb-line idea), because an upright wall is perpendicular to the floor. [2 marks — accept any correct explanation linking upright walls to a 90° construction.]
(d) Correct segment and perpendicular bisector [1]; the bisector meets the segment at its midpoint (each half 5 cm), at right angles [1].
Note: Constructions should be assessed for clear arcs and construction lines, neatness and accuracy. Measured angles may be accepted within ±2° of the required value. Award no marks where a protractor replaces a required compass-and-ruler construction.

Easy items secure definitions, bisection facts and recognition of constructions; the higher-demand items (A14, A22, A24, B3(c), B5 and the multi-step parts of B6) require reasoning about equidistance, choosing the correct bisection route to 75°, and repeated bisection.
QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY
Check
Outcome
Curriculum scope
All 46 items trace to B7.3.1.2 (indicators .1–.7) only. No NaCCA indicators were invented; constructing triangles from given data, loci, scale drawing and circle theorems were excluded as out of scope for this standard.
Class appropriateness
JHS 1 (Basic 7) level: perpendiculars, perpendicular bisectors, copying/bisecting angles, and constructing 90°, 45°, 60°, 30°, 15° and 75° with compasses and ruler, plus environmental examples.
BECE style
Section A uses 4-option MCQs with one defensible answer; Section B uses genuine construction tasks with mark allocation and verification expectations, set partly in Ghanaian contexts (classrooms, roof frames, masons, crates).
Curriculum exemplars
Every text-based exemplar of B7.3.1.2 is used: copying RS = PQ and erecting/dropping perpendiculars (B1); AB = 8 cm and AB = 5.5 cm bisections (B2); copying angle A and bisecting ∠ABC (B3); 90°→45° and 60°→30° chains (B4); 15°, 75° and bisecting 75° (B5); buildings, water tanks and boxes as environmental sources (B6).
Application & reasoning
21% of marks sit at Analyse/Create level; the equidistance property (A14), the 75° construction route (A22, B5b) and repeated bisection (A28, B3c, B5c) carry the higher-order demand.
MCQ distractors
All distractors model common learner errors: compass width less than half the segment (A11-C/B), arcs from one end only (A13-A), confusing angle bisector with perpendicular bisector (A31-B/C), halving the wrong angle (A18-B/C, A23-A/C), and subtracting instead of halving lengths (A10-A, A15-D).
Answer key verified
Every length and angle value was recomputed programmatically; all 46 keys confirmed correct.
Key balance & randomness
A = 11, B = 10, C = 9, D = 10; no consecutive correct letters repeat, so no answer pattern exists.
Marking consistency
Section A = 40 × 1 mark; Section B = 6 × 10 marks (each question’s parts verified to sum to 10); grand total 100 marks.
Language
Clear Ghanaian school English; BECE terminology used (“perpendicular bisector”, “angle bisector”, “erect/drop a perpendicular”, “construction lines”, “bisect”).
Originality
Except the curriculum exemplar structures noted above (public NaCCA materials), all items are original compositions for this mock; none is reproduced from WAEC/BECE past questions or any textbook.
Prepared in line with the NaCCA Common Core Programme (Mathematics, JHS 1) — Strand 3: Geometry and Measurement, Sub-Strand 1: Shape and Space (B7.3.1.2).

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Perimeters in mixed units (B7.3.2.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 7 cm 5 mm = 7.5 cm [1]; (ii) 1 m 75 cm = 1.75 m [1]; (iii) 2 km 300 m = 2300 m [1]. (Curriculum exemplars E.g.2 and E.g.3.)
(b) 4 cm 5 mm = 4.5 cm and 5 cm 5 mm = 5.5 cm [1]; perimeter = 3 + 4.5 + 5.5 = 13 cm [2 marks].
(c) (i) 2 × (120 + 80) = 400 m [2 marks]; (ii) 400 × GH₵2.50 = GH₵1000.00 [2 marks].
Question 2 — Parts of a circle and the value of π (B7.3.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) radius [1]; (ii) diameter [1]; (iii) circumference [1]; (iv) arc [1]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.1: parts of a circle.)
(b) (i) Tin A: 13 ÷ 4 = 3.25 [1]; Tin B: 38 ÷ 12 = 3.17 [1]. (ii) The values of c ÷ d are all nearly the same, approximately 3.14; this constant ratio is called π [2 marks]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.3.)
(c) (i) 22/7 [1]; (ii) 3.142 [1]. Accept 3.141592+ shown to 3 d.p.
Question 3 — Circumference of a circle (B7.3.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) C = 2πr [1]; (ii) C = πd [1].
(b) (i) d = 2 × 140 = 280 cm [2 marks]; (ii) C = 2 × (22/7) × 140 = 880 cm [2 marks]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.4 i.)
(c) C = 2 × 3.142 × 5 = 31.42 ≈ 31.4 cm. [2 marks: 1 for the multiplication, 1 for rounding to the nearest tenth.] (Curriculum exemplar E.g.4 ii.)
(d) d = 88 × 7 ÷ 22 = 28 cm. [2 marks]
Question 4 — Solving problems with circumference (B7.3.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) C = 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 88 m. [3 marks: 1 for the formula/substitution, 2 for the correct value.]
(b) Distance in one turn = circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 35 = 220 cm. [3 marks]
(c) C = 3.142 × 10 = 31.42 m (accept 31.4 m). [2 marks]
(d) r = 132 × 7 ÷ 44 = 21 cm. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Drawing on square grids (B7.3.2.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Neat rectangle 6 units by 4 units [2 marks]; area = 6 × 4 = 24 square units [1].
(b) Area = 2 × 24 = 48 square units [1]; correct rectangle drawn [1]; one valid dimension pair stated, e.g. 8 units × 6 units (or 12 × 4, 16 × 3, 24 × 2) [1]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.1 i.)
(c) Correct triangle drawn on the grid [2 marks]; base and height stated, e.g. base 6 units and height 1 unit (or base 2 units and height 3 units) [1]; explanation: ½ × base × height = ½ × 6 × 1 = 3 square units [1]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.2.)
Question 6 — Mixed problems  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 2 m 40 cm = 2.4 m and 1 m 60 cm = 1.6 m [2 marks]; (ii) perimeter = 2 × (2.4 + 1.6) = 8 m [2 marks].
(b) C = 2 × (22/7) × 3.5 = 22 cm. [3 marks]
(c) Example: “A circular bowl has radius 7 cm. Find its circumference.” C = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm. [3 marks: 2 for a sensible circumference problem; 1 for the correct solution.] Accept any correct equivalent.
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. In circumference work, accept answers obtained with π = 3.142 where 22/7 was required only if the question permitted a choice of π. Grid drawings must be drawn on the grid lines; areas are counted in square units.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Deriving the formula (B7.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Area of rectangle = 8 × 5 = 40 cm² [2 marks]; each triangle = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm² [1].
(b) Two identical triangles form a rectangle/parallelogram of area base × height [2]; so one triangle is half of that: ½ × base × height [1]. (Follows the curriculum derivation: triangle = half of rectangle/parallelogram.)
(c) (i) 12 × 6 = 72 cm² [2]; (ii) 72 ÷ 2 = 36 cm² [2].
Question 2 — Calculating areas (B7.3.2.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm² [2]; (b) ½ × 12 × 9 = 54 cm² [2]; (c) ½ × 7 × 4 = 14 cm² [2]; (d) ½ × 6 × 8 = 24 cm² [2]; (e) ½ × 4.2 × 5 = 10.5 cm² [2]. Award 1 mark only if the working is shown but the answer is wrong.
Question 3 — Finding missing dimensions (B7.3.2.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) h = 2 × 24 ÷ 8 = 6 cm [2]; (b) b = 2 × 50 ÷ 10 = 10 cm [2]; (c) b = 2 × 42 ÷ 7 = 12 cm [2]; (d) h = 2 × 36 ÷ 9 = 8 cm [2]; (e) b = 2 × 60 ÷ 12 = 10 cm [2].
Question 4 — Areas on square grids (B7.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 6 + ½ × 8 = 6 + 4 = 10 square units. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar E.g.1: counting unit squares.)
(b) Triangle drawn with base 6 units and height 4 units [2]; area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 square units [2].
(c) A different triangle of area 12 square units drawn, e.g. base 4 units and height 6 units [2]; explanation: both have ½ × base × height = 12, so the areas are equal even though the shapes differ [2].
Question 5 — Area problems in real life  [10 marks]
(a) ½ × 30 × 20 = 300 cm². [2 marks]
(b) Area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 m² [2]; cost = 30 × GH₵2.00 = GH₵60.00 [2].
(c) Rectangle: 10 × 4 = 40 cm² [1]; triangle: ½ × 10 × 3 = 15 cm² [1]; total = 40 + 15 = 55 cm² [2].
Question 6 — Creating and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) Example: base 6 cm and height 6 cm [2]; check: ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 cm² [2]. Accept any pair with base × height = 36.
(b) Area of square = 10 × 10 = 100 cm² [1]; each triangle = 100 ÷ 4 = 25 cm² [2].
(c) No [1]; triangles with the same base and height have equal areas but can have different shapes, e.g. the top vertex can be moved along a line parallel to the base [2]. Accept any correct example.
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Areas must be given in square units. Accept any mathematically correct dimensions in creation tasks provided the required area is verified.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Bearings (B7.3.2.3.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) North [1]; (ii) clockwise [1]; (iii) three figures [1]. (Curriculum: true bearings measured clockwise from North.)
(b) (i) 090° [1]; (ii) 180° [1]; (iii) 270° [1].
(c) 060°. [2 marks]
(d) The ship moves a distance of 3 km in a direction 60° clockwise from the North line. [2 marks — 1 for the distance, 1 for the direction.] (Curriculum exemplar: vector as (distance, bearing).)
Question 2 — Back bearings (B7.3.2.3.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) add 180° [1]; (ii) subtract 180° [1].
(b) 060° + 180° = 240°. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar E.g.2.)
(c) 145° + 180° = 325°. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar E.g.3.)
(d) 200° − 180° = 020°. [2 marks]
(e) 275° − 180° = 095°. [2 marks]
Question 3 — Scalar and vector quantities (B7.3.2.3.3)  [10 marks]
(a) A scalar quantity has magnitude (size) only [1]; a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction [1].
(b) Vector quantities: weight, force, velocity, momentum [3 marks for the full correct group]; scalar quantities: time, speed, distance, mass, volume, energy, work [2 marks for the full correct group]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.2.)
(c) (i) (3 km, 060°) [1]; (ii) (5 km, 120°) [1]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.4.)
(d) Any valid example, e.g. the wind blowing at 20 km/h from the North, displacement of a walk, velocity of a trotro. [1 mark]
Question 4 — Vectors in column form (B7.3.2.3.4)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) (2, 3) [1]; (ii) (−3, 4) [1].
(b) (i) 2 units East and 3 units North [2]; (ii) 3 units West and 4 units North [2].
(c) (5, 2). [2 marks]
(d) 4 units/km West and 3 units/km North. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Magnitude of vectors (B7.3.2.3.5)  [10 marks]
(a) √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. [2 marks: 1 for the Pythagoras set-up.]
(b) √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13. [2 marks]
(c) √((−3)² + 4²) = √25 = 5. [2 marks]
(d) √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 km. [2 marks]
(e) √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 km. [2 marks]
Question 6 — Mixed problems  [10 marks]
(a) (i) √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 km [2]; (ii) 7 km is the total distance walked along the two sides, but the straight-line (displacement) distance is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle formed, which is 5 km [2].
(b) Example: “A cyclist goes 6 km East and then 8 km North.” [1]; straight-line distance √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 km [2]. Accept any correct journey matching (6, 8).
(c) (i) 110° + 180° = 290° [2]; (ii) (5 km, 290°) [1].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Bearings must be written as three figures (e.g. 060°, not 60°). Accept any mathematically correct journey or example in creation tasks.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Reflectional (fold) symmetry (B7.3.3.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) A shape has reflectional (fold) symmetry if it can be folded along a line so that the two halves match exactly. [2 marks]
(b) (i) 4 [1]; (ii) 2 [1]; (iii) 3 [1]; (iv) unlimited / infinitely many [1].
(c) Any two valid examples, e.g. adinkra symbols, kente patterns, a leaf, a butterfly, a letter such as A or M, a window frame. [2 marks]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.1: adinkra symbols.)
(d) Correct square shaded so that a line of symmetry exists [1]; explanation of the mirror line used [1]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.2.)
Question 2 — Reflection in the coordinate plane (B7.3.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Points A(3, 1), B(3, 3), C(4, 3) plotted correctly and joined [3 marks — 1 per point]. (Points follow the curriculum exemplar for B7.3.3.1.2.)
(b) A′(3, −1) [1]; B′(3, −3) [1]; C′(4, −3) [1]; image drawn correctly [1].
(c) D′(2, 3). [2 marks]
(d) Any two: the image is congruent to the object; corresponding points are equal distances from the mirror line on opposite sides; orientation is reversed. [1 mark]
Question 3 — Translation by vectors (B7.3.3.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) A translation is a slide of every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction, without turning or flipping [2]; example: people going down a slide, a lift moving, pushing a desk across the floor [1]. (Curriculum exemplar E.g.1: the slide.)
(b) (2 + 4, 3 + 1) = (6, 4). [2 marks]
(c) (5 − 3, 2 + 2) = (2, 4). [2 marks]
(d) (5 − 2, 6 − 2) = (3, 4). [3 marks: 1 for each component and 1 for the vector form.]
Question 4 — Congruent and similar shapes (B7.3.3.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) Congruent shapes have the same shape and the same size [1]; similar shapes have the same shape but may be different sizes [1].
(b) Similar: yes, because 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2, so the corresponding sides are in the same ratio [2]; congruent: no, because the sizes are different [2].
(c) Any two valid examples, e.g. matching tiles in a carpet design, repeated motifs in kente cloth, identical windows, a photo and its enlargement (similar). [2 marks]. (Curriculum exemplar: carpet designs, fabric patterns.)
(d) Yes [1]; each side of the second triangle is 2 times the matching side of the first (2:4, 3:6, 4:8), so the sides are in proportion [1].
Question 5 — Mixed coordinate transformations  [10 marks]
(a) Points P(1, 1), Q(4, 1), R(1, 3) plotted and joined correctly. [2 marks]
(b) P′(3, 4), Q′(6, 4), R′(3, 6). [4 marks: 1 per coordinate and 1 for all three correct.]
(c) P′(−1, 1), Q′(−4, 1), R′(−1, 3). [4 marks: 1 per coordinate and 1 for all three correct.]
Question 6 — Creating and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) Any correct symmetric grid design [2]; line(s) of symmetry stated correctly [2]. Accept any valid creation.
(b) Example: point (1, 2) translated by (3, −1) gives image (1 + 3, 2 − 1) = (4, 1). [3 marks: 1 for the point, 1 for the vector, 1 for the correct image.] Accept any correct choice.
(c) (i) Similar [1]; (ii) the enlargement has the same shape but every length is doubled, so corresponding lengths are in the ratio 1 : 2; the shapes are not the same size, so they are not congruent [2].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Plots and images on the coordinate plane must be read and written as (x, y). Accept any mathematically correct design, point or vector in creation tasks.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Data collection (B7.4.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Data collection is the process of gathering facts, figures or information (data) to answer a question or solve a problem. [2 marks]
(b) Quantitative data can be counted or measured and is expressed in numbers [1], e.g. the number of desks, height, bus fare [1]; qualitative data describes qualities or opinions and is not numerical [1], e.g. favourite subject, favourite day of the week [1].
(c) (i) Questionnaire (or survey), because the opinions of many students can be collected quickly and directly [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for justification]. (Curriculum exemplar: drinks for a class party.)
(ii) Observation and counting, because the desks can simply be counted and recorded in each classroom [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for justification]. (Curriculum exemplar: number of desks.)
Question 2 — Questionnaires (B7.4.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) A questionnaire is a set of written questions given to people (respondents) in order to collect data. [2 marks]
(b) Any four sensible questions about snacks [3 marks], with at least one collecting quantitative data, e.g. “How many times a week do you buy snacks?” [1 mark]. Example set: 1) What is your name? 2) What is your favourite snack? 3) Tick one: mango / biscuit / groundnut / other. 4) How much do you spend on snacks each day?
(c) Any two: clear and easy to understand; short and focused (one idea per question); not leading; provides space or choices for answering; polite. [2 marks]
(d) Any two reasons: it is a leading question that pushes the respondent towards saying yes [1]; it is closed to one side / ambiguous, so the answer will be biased [1]. [2 marks]
Question 3 — From questionnaire to graph (B7.4.1.1.2 & B7.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Correct tallies and frequencies: Mathematics //// = 5; Science /// = 3; English // = 2; ICT / = 1. [4 marks: 1 for each correct row including the tally.]
(b) Bar chart: labelled axes (subject and frequency) [1]; bars drawn to correct heights 5, 3, 2, 1 [2]; equal bar widths with gaps [1].
(c) Any valid conclusion, e.g. Mathematics is the most popular subject, or more than half of the 10 students chose Mathematics or Science. [2 marks]. (Curriculum exemplar: write a conclusion and/or pose questions on the graph.)
Question 4 — Reading a frequency table (B7.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 2 + 6 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 20 students. [2 marks]
(b) Mark 2, obtained by 6 students (the greatest frequency). [2 marks]
(c) Marks 3, 4 and 5: 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 students. [3 marks: 1 for selecting the correct marks and 2 for the sum.]
(d) Bar chart: labelled axes [1]; bars to heights 2, 6, 4, 5, 3 [1]; equal widths with gaps [1].
Question 5 — Pie chart (B7.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Total = 40. Football: 16/40 × 360° = 144° [1]; Volleyball: 10/40 × 360° = 90° [1]; Athletics: 8/40 × 360° = 72° [1]; Handball: 6/40 × 360° = 54° [1]. (Structure follows the curriculum’s 40-household pie chart exemplar.)
(b) Circle drawn with correct sectors (angles 144°, 90°, 72°, 54°) [2]; sectors labelled with sport names (or key) [1].
(c) Football [1]; fraction = 16/40 = 2/5 [2 marks: 1 for 16/40 and 1 for simplifying to 2/5].
Question 6 — Creating and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) One clear, answerable survey question [1]; a suitable method chosen (questionnaire, observation, etc.) [1]; two convincing justifications linking the method to the question [2]. Accept any valid survey plan.
(b) Key “one symbol = 5 students” stated [1]; Mathematics club 3 symbols, Science club 2 symbols, Debate club 2 symbols, labelled [2].
(c) Temperature changes continuously over time [1]; a line graph joins the points so increases and decreases are easy to see [1]; the horizontal axis can show the days of the week and the vertical axis the temperatures [1].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically correct questions, surveys, conclusions or designs. Graphs must have labelled axes and correct scales.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — The mean (B7.4.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) The mean is the sum of all the values in a data set divided by the number of values. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar: divide the sum of the items by the number of items.)
(b) Sum = 12 + 15 + 18 + 11 + 16 + 18 = 90 [2]; mean = 90 ÷ 6 = 15 [2].
(c) Sum = 45 + 52 + 48 + 55 + 50 = 250 [2]; mean = 250 ÷ 5 = 50 kg [2].
Question 2 — The median (B7.4.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) The median is the middle value of a data set when the values are arranged in order [2]; first step: arrange the values in ascending (or descending) order [1].
(b) Array: 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 18, 20 [2]; eight values (even), so median = mean of the 4th and 5th values = (16 + 17) ÷ 2 = 16.5 [2].
(c) With an even number of values there is no single middle value [1]; the two middle values are equally central, so their mean is taken to represent the centre [2].
Question 3 — The mode  [10 marks]
(a) The mode is the value that occurs most often in a data set. [2 marks]
(b) The value 2 occurs three times (more than any other), so the mode is 2. [2 marks]
(c) The mode [1]; because it gives the size that occurs most often / is demanded by most customers, so it tells him which size will sell fastest [2]. (Mean or median sizes could be values he cannot sell.)
(d) 9 occurs twice, every other value occurs once, so the mode is 9. [3 marks: 1 for identifying 9 repeats and 2 for the correct conclusion.]
Question 4 — Central tendency from a frequency table (curriculum exemplar structure)  [10 marks]
(a) Σfx = 1×2 + 2×6 + 3×4 + 4×5 + 5×3 = 2 + 12 + 12 + 20 + 15 = 61 [2]; n = 2 + 6 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 20 [1]; mean = 61 ÷ 20 = 3.05 [1].
(b) There are 20 values, so the 10th and 11th values are the middle values [1]; running through the frequencies (2, 8, 12, 17, 20), both the 10th and 11th values are 3 [1]; median = 3 [1].
(c) Mark 2 has the greatest frequency (6), so the modal mark is 2. [3 marks]
Question 5 — Solving problems with the mean (B7.4.1.2.1, curriculum exemplars)  [10 marks]
(a) Sum = 25 + 48 + 25 + 33 + 57 + 50 = 238 [1]; mean = 238 ÷ 6 = 39⅔ ≈ 39.7 loaves per day [2]. (Curriculum exemplar: the shopkeeper’s loaves.)
(b) Required total = 6 × 85 = 510 [1]; sum of the five scores = 75 + 87 + 90 + 88 + 79 = 419 [1]; sixth score = 510 − 419 = 91 [2]. (Curriculum exemplar: Sena’s scores.)
(c) Required total = 6 × 14 = 84 [1]; sixth number = 84 − 79 = 5 [2].
Question 6 — Creating and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) Any five values summing to 35, e.g. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 [2]; check shown: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 [1]. Accept any valid set.
(b) Any five values whose middle (3rd) value when ordered is 10, e.g. 4, 8, 10, 12, 15. [3 marks] Accept any valid set.
(c) Mean = (25 + 30 + 35 + 90) ÷ 4 = 180 ÷ 4 = 45 [1]; median = (30 + 35) ÷ 2 = 32.5 [1]; the median better represents the group [1] because 90 is an outlier that pulls the mean up to 45, which is older than three of the four people [1].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically valid data set in the creation tasks. Workings must show the sum (or Σfx) and the division.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Classifying likelihood (B7.4.2.1.1 & B7.4.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Impossible [1]; a die has faces 1 to 6 only, so 7 cannot appear [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(b) Certain [1]; Tuesday always follows Monday in the order of the days of the week [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(c) Possible [1]; it may or may not rain — it is not guaranteed, but it is not ruled out [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(d) Impossible [1]; the greatest possible total on two dice is 6 + 6 = 12, so 13 cannot occur [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(e) Possible [1]; the baby could be a girl or a boy — neither outcome is certain nor impossible [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
Question 2 — Sample space (B7.4.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of a probability experiment. [2 marks]
(b) Sample space: HH, HT, TH, TT [3 marks: 2 for the full list, 1 for order/notation]; number of outcomes = 4 [1].
(c) Sample space: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} [1]; number of outcomes = 6 [1].
(d) Sample space: {red, blue} [1]; number of outcomes = 2 [1].
Question 3 — Calculating probability with a die (B7.4.2.1.3)  [10 marks]
Each probability = favourable outcomes ÷ 6.
(a) P(4) = 1/6. [2 marks]
(b) Even numbers: 2, 4, 6 → P = 3/6 = 1/2. [2 marks]
(c) Multiples of 3: 3, 6 → P = 2/6 = 1/3. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar.)
(d) A 3 or greater: 3, 4, 5, 6 → P = 4/6 = 2/3. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar.)
(e) Factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6 → P = 4/6 = 2/3. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar.)
Question 4 — Expressing probabilities in different forms (B7.4.2.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 1/4 = 0.25 [2]; (ii) 25% [2].
(b) (i) 1/2 [1]; (ii) 0.5 [1]; (iii) 50% [1]; (iv) 1 : 2 [1]. (Structure follows the curriculum’s fraction/decimal/percentage/ratio table.)
(c) P(red) = 1/4 [1] = 25% [1].
Question 5 — Probability from a bag  [10 marks]
(a) 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 fruits. [2 marks]
(b) P(orange) = 3/10. [2 marks]
(c) Not a mango = oranges + bananas = 3 + 5 = 8 fruits [1]; P = 8/10 [1] = 4/5 [1].
(d) Banana [1]; there are more bananas (5) than any other fruit, so 5/10 is the greatest probability [2].
Question 6 — Creating and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) 2 sectors should be red [2]; because 2/8 = 1/4, so 2 red sectors out of 8 give the required probability [2]. Accept any equivalent design with correct justification.
(b) Example: 3 blue and 2 red counters (5 counters in total) [2]; P(blue) = 3/5, so the condition is satisfied [1]. Accept any 3k blue and 2k red.
(c) An event that cannot happen has 0 favourable outcomes, giving probability 0 [1]; an event that is certain has all outcomes favourable, giving probability 1 [1]; every other event has some but not all outcomes favourable, so its probability lies between 0 and 1 [1].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Probabilities should be given as fractions in their simplest form unless another form is requested. Classifications must be supported by a reason.

No content outside the supplied curriculum (e.g. experimental vs theoretical probability, two-event combined sample spaces beyond simple listing, or probability trees) was introduced.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Place value of numbers greater than 1,000,000,000  [10 marks]
(a) Four billion, seventy-three million, six hundred and five thousand, two hundred and eighteen. [2 marks: full answer; award 1 mark if any one complete group is written correctly.]
(b) Ten millions. [1 mark]
(c) 5,000 (five thousand). [1 mark]
(d) 4,000,000,000 + 70,000,000 + 3,000,000 + 600,000 + 5,000 + 200 + 10 + 8. [2 marks for completely correct expansion; 1 mark for up to two wrong/missing terms.]
(e) 6. [1 mark]
(f) Value of digit 7 = 70,000,000 and value of digit 3 = 3,000,000 [1 mark for either correct value]; Difference = 70,000,000 − 3,000,000 = 67,000,000 [1 mark for the correct difference].
(g) 4,074,000,000. [1 mark — the hundred thousands digit 6 means we round up.]
Question 2 — Rounding whole numbers greater than 1,000,000,000  [10 marks]
Award 1 mark for identifying the correct deciding digit/rounding direction (method) and 1 mark for the correct answer in (a)–(d).
(a) GH₵7,935,000,000 (hundred thousands digit is 5, so round up). [2 marks]
(b) GH₵3,059,400,000 (ten thousands digit is 4, so round down). [2 marks]
(c) GH₵5,996,700,000 (thousands digit is 3, so round down). [2 marks]
(d) GH₵2,480,365,500 (tens digit is 8, so round up). [2 marks]
(e) City Transport Ltd [1 mark]. Reason: GH₵5,996,703,000 is closer to GH₵6,000,000,000 than to GH₵5,900,000,000 (or: its ten millions digit 9 makes it round up to the next hundred million) [1 mark]. Accept any correct equivalent explanation.
Question 3 — Rounding decimals; decimal places and significant figures  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 24.8  (ii) 24.77  (iii) 24.765. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) (i) 0.81  (ii) 0.807. [1 mark each = 2 marks]
(c) (i) 4 decimal places  (ii) 6 significant figures. [1 mark each = 2 marks]
(d) 0.050 m. [1 mark. Accept 0.05, but 0.050 is the preferred 2-significant-figure form.]
(e) 10.00. [1 mark. Accept 10, but 10.00 shows the required 2 decimal places.]
(f) 2.347 litres. [1 mark]
Question 4 — Comparing and ordering numbers greater than 1,000,000,000  [10 marks]
(a) (i) <  (ii) >  (iii) <  (iv) > . [1 mark each = 4 marks]
(b) 4,056,000,000; 4,065,000,000; 4,506,000,000; 4,560,000,000. [3 marks for the completely correct order; 1 mark if only the two smallest numbers are correctly identified and placed.]
(c) Ashanti; Greater Accra; Western; Eastern. [3 marks for the completely correct order; 1 mark for correctly identifying only the region with the highest amount.]
Question 5 — Integrated application in a Ghanaian context  [10 marks]
(a) Twelve billion, four hundred and six million, three hundred and eighty-five thousand cedis. [2 marks: 1 mark for the billions and millions groups correct; 1 mark for the thousands group correct.]
(b) (i) GH₵12,406,000,000  (ii) GH₵12,406,400,000. [1 mark each = 2 marks]
(c) 12,399,999,999 < 12,406,385,000 [1 mark]; the amount spent was less than the budget [1 mark].
(d) GH₵12,400,000,000. [2 marks: 1 mark for keeping the first three significant figures (1, 2, 4); 1 mark for the correct zeros after rounding.]
(e) 12,000,000,000 + 400,000,000 + 6,000,000 + 300,000 + 80,000 + 5,000. [2 marks for completely correct expansion; 1 mark for up to two wrong/missing terms.]
Question 6 — Problem solving and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 9,876,543,210  (ii) 1,023,456,789. [1 mark each = 2 marks]
(b) 9,876,543,210 − 1,023,456,789 = 8,853,086,421. [3 marks: 1 mark for writing the subtraction correctly; 1 mark for a correct subtraction process, including borrowing/exchanging; 1 mark for the correct answer.]
(c) 8,853,100,000. [2 marks: 1 method + 1 correct answer — the ten thousands digit 8 makes us round up.]
(d) 8,900,000,000. [1 mark]
(e) Any correct explanation, for example: A number that begins with 0 is not a ten-digit number, because the first zero has no value. 0,987,654,321 is actually 987,654,321, a nine-digit number, which is less than 1,000,000,000. [2 marks: 1 mark for stating that the number would not be a ten-digit number; 1 mark for a correct justification.]
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically correct method unless the question specifies otherwise.

Question 1 — Multiplying and dividing by powers of 10  [10 marks]

(a) (i) Commutative property of addition [1]; (ii) Associative property of multiplication [1]; (iii) Distributive property of multiplication [1].

(e) 4 × GH₵25.00 = GH₵100.00; change = GH₵200.00 − GH₵100.00 = GH₵100.00. [1 mark]
Question 3 — Addition and subtraction of whole numbers  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 4,728 + 3,695 = 8,423 [2 marks: 1 for a correct vertical method, 1 for the answer]; (ii) 8,003 − 2,647 = 5,356 [2 marks].
(b) 8,196 − 2,384 = 5,812, so the missing digit is 8. [2 marks: 1 for the subtraction/inverse; 1 for the digit.]
(c) (i) 6,275 + 4,849 = 11,124 eggs [1]; (ii) 11,124 − 3,650 = 7,474 eggs [1].
(d) 3,968 ≈ 4,000 and 2,415 ≈ 2,400 [1]; estimate = 4,000 + 2,400 = 6,400 [1].
Question 4 — Multiplication and division of multi-digit numbers  [10 marks]
In (a)–(e): award 1 mark for a correct method/process and 1 mark for the correct answer.
(a) 5,437 × 6 = 32,622. [2 marks]
(b) 736 × 45 = (736 × 40) + (736 × 5) = 29,440 + 3,680 = 33,120. [2 marks]
(c) 4,692 ÷ 12 = 391. [2 marks]
(d) 2,014 ÷ 8 = 251 remainder 6. [2 marks]
(e) 3,240 ÷ 24 = 135 oranges in each basket. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Story problems involving decimals (NaCCA exemplars for B7.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Mrs Anderson: 13.6 − 2.4 = 11.2 kg [2 marks]; Altogether: 13.6 + 11.2 = 24.8 kg [2 marks]. Accept equivalent correct methods, e.g. (2 × 13.6) − 2.4 = 24.8 kg.
(b) Father: 28.6 × 4 = 114.4 kg [2 marks]; Total: 28.6 + 114.4 = 143 kg [1 mark].
(c) 45.75 ÷ 5 = 9.15 m. [3 marks: 1 for setting up the division; 1 for the correct process; 1 for the answer.]
Question 6 — Creating and solving decimal story problems  [10 marks]
(a) Example: “Yaa buys 4 packets of sugar at GH₵15.50 each. How much does she pay altogether?” Answer: 15.5 × 4 = GH₵62.00. [3 marks: 1 for an appropriate story context; 1 for using the correct operation; 1 for the correct answer.] Accept any sensible story.
(b) Fish sold: 48.9 + 36.65 = 85.55 kg [1]; fish left: 125.75 − 85.55 = 40.2 kg [2]. Accept a correct stage-by-stage subtraction: 125.75 − 48.9 = 76.85, then 76.85 − 36.65 = 40.2 kg.
(c) GH₵77.40 ÷ 12 = GH₵6.45. [2 marks]
(d) Example: “Kofi saves GH₵2.50 every day. How much does he save in 40 days?” Answer: 2.5 × 40 = GH₵100.00. [2 marks: 1 for an appropriate story; 1 for the correct answer.] Accept any story that correctly uses 2.5 × 40 (or 2.5 × 4 × 10).

Outcome
Curriculum scope
All 46 items trace to B7.1.2.1 (incl. .1, .2, .3) and B7.1.2.2 (incl. .1, .2, .3) only. No NaCCA indicators were invented; no out-of-scope content (e.g. fractions beyond benchmark fractions, negative numbers, percentages) was introduced.
Class appropriateness
JHS 1 (Basic 7) level: addition/subtraction limited to four-digit operands; multiplication/division by 1- and 2-digit numbers only; decimals handled across all four operations as specified.
BECE style
Section A uses 4-option MCQs with one defensible answer; Section B uses numbered parts with mark allocation and worked-response expectations, in Ghanaian contexts (cedis, market, farming, transport, school).
Curriculum exemplars
Question 5 reproduces the three exemplars attached to B7.1.2.2 in the supplied brief (Mrs Adamu/Mrs Anderson; Ebo and his father; Mrs Armah’s linen), ensuring direct alignment with the curriculum; all other items are original.
Application & reasoning
25% of marks sit at Analyse/Create level; mental-maths strategies (compensation, doubling-and-halving, distributive property, estimation) are explicitly assessed rather than only rote procedures.
MCQ distractors
All distractors model common learner errors: wrong decimal-point shift (A1–A5, A39), place-value slips in 4-digit work (A19–A24), quotient-place errors (A27–A31), and decimal story-problem mis-steps such as finding only one person’s amount (A33–A35).
Answer key verified
Every product, quotient, sum, difference and decimal operation was recomputed programmatically; all 46 keys confirmed correct.
Key balance & randomness
A = 9, B = 10, C = 11, D = 10; no consecutive correct letters repeat, so no answer pattern exists.
Marking consistency
Section A = 40 × 1 mark; Section B = 6 × 10 marks (each question’s parts verified to sum to 10); grand total 100 marks.
Language
Clear Ghanaian school English; BECE terminology used (“evaluate”, “work out mentally”, “altogether”, “share equally”); cedi sign GH₵ used throughout.
Originality
Except the three B7.1.2.2 curriculum exemplars noted above, all items are original compositions for this mock; none is reproduced from WAEC/BECE past questions or any textbook.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Meaning of repeated factors (B7.1.2.3.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 4⁵   (ii) 9²   (iii) 2⁷. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) (i) 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 [2 marks: 1 for the correct expansion, 1 for the value]; (ii) 6³ = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 [2 marks].
(c) (i) 6 × 6 = 36 bottle tops [1]; (ii) 6² [1].
(d) Base = 11, exponent (index) = 5. [1 mark]
Question 2 — Expressing numbers as products of powers (B7.1.2.3.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 32 = 2⁵   (ii) 729 = 3⁶   (iii) 100,000 = 10⁵. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) 3³ × 5². [2 marks: 1 mark for each correct power.]
(c) (i) 2³ × 5² = 8 × 25 = 200 [2 marks: 1 for evaluating the powers, 1 for the product]; (ii) 3² × 2⁴ = 9 × 16 = 144 [2 marks].
(d) 72 = 2³ × 3². [1 mark]
Question 3 — The zero exponent (B7.1.2.3.3)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 1   (ii) 1   (iii) 1. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) (i) 1 + 1 = 2   (ii) 6 × 1 = 6   (iii) 1 × 1 = 1. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(c) From the pattern, each step divides by 2: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, so 2⁰ = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 [1 mark]. Explanation: the same reasoning applies to any natural number, so any natural number with zero as its exponent is 1 [1 mark]. Accept any correct demonstration, e.g. 5² ÷ 5² = 1, and 5² ÷ 5² = 5⁰, hence 5⁰ = 1.
(d) (i) n = 0   (ii) n = 3. [1 mark each = 2 marks]
Question 4 — Value of numbers in index form (B7.1.2.3.4)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 4⁴ = 256   (ii) 5⁴ = 625   (iii) 10⁵ = 100,000. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) 7³ = 7 × 7 × 7 = 49 × 7 = 343. [2 marks for all four entries correct; 1 mark for one error. The completion follows the style of the curriculum exemplar 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125.]
(c) 3⁵ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 243 and 5³ = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 [1 mark]; since 243 > 125, 3⁵ is larger [1 mark].
(d) (i) 16 + 27 = 43   (ii) 100 − 36 = 64. [1 mark each = 2 marks]
(e) 8, because 8³ = 512. [1 mark]
Question 5 — HCF by the product of prime factors (B7.1.2.3.5)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 [1]; (ii) 90 = 2 × 3² × 5 [1].
(b) Common prime factors: 2, 3 and 5, each taken with its lowest power: 2¹ × 3¹ × 5¹ [2 marks]; HCF = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 [1 mark].
(c) 48 = 2⁴ × 3 and 72 = 2³ × 3² [1 mark]; HCF = 2³ × 3 [1 mark] = 24 [1 mark].
(d) (i) Greatest number of packs = HCF(48, 72) = 24 packs [1]; (ii) 48 ÷ 24 = 2 pencils in each pack [1].
Question 6 — Integrated problems and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) Example: “Kofi arranges bottle tops into 3 heaps of 3 caps each. How many bottle tops does he have altogether?” Answer: 3² = 9 bottle tops. [3 marks: 1 for an appropriate story using counting objects; 1 for the correct operation; 1 for the correct answer.] Accept any sensible story that uses 3².
(b) Area = 23² [1] = 529 m² [1].
(c) 2ⁿ = 32 gives n = 5; 5ᵐ = 1 gives m = 0 [1 mark]; n + m = 5 + 0 = 5 [1 mark].
(d) 6⁰ = 1 and 6¹ = 6, so 6⁰ + 6¹ = 1 + 6 = 7. [1 mark]
(e) Take each common prime factor with its lowest power: 2³ × 5 [1 mark]; HCF = 2³ × 5 (= 40) [1 mark]. The factor 7 is not common, so it is not included.
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically correct method unless the question specifies otherwise. Index-form answers must show correct superscript notation.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Benchmark fractions, percentages and decimals (B7.1.3.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 50%   (ii) 60%   (iii) 35%. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) (i) 0.25   (ii) 0.666… (0.6̇; recurring)   (iii) 0.45. [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(c) 3/4 = 0.75 = 75% [2 marks: 1 for the decimal, 1 for the percentage]; 0.2 = 1/5 = 20% [1 mark].
(d) Divide the rectangle into 6 equal parts and shade 5 of them. [1 mark]
Question 2 — Comparing and ordering (B7.1.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 3/4 > 5/8 (0.75 vs 0.625)   (ii) 0.99 > 0.977   (iii) 40% > 3/8 (0.4 vs 0.375). [1 mark each = 3 marks]
(b) LCM of 6, 4 and 8 is 24: 5/6 = 20/24, 3/4 = 18/24, 7/8 = 21/24 [2 marks for correct conversion]; descending order: 7/8, 5/6, 3/4 [1 mark]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(c) 0.098, 0.123, 0.985. [2 marks for fully correct order; 1 mark if only the least is correctly identified.] (Curriculum exemplar.)
(d) 25% = 0.25, 1/3 ≈ 0.333, 0.3 = 0.3, so ascending order is 25%, 0.3, 1/3 [1 mark for order, 1 mark for the conversions/reason].
Question 3 — Addition and subtraction of fractions (B7.1.3.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6 [2 marks: 1 for the common denominator, 1 for the answer]; (ii) 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12 [2 marks].
(b) 2 2/5 + 1 2/3 = (2 + 1) + (2/5 + 2/3) = 3 + 6/15 + 10/15 = 3 16/15 = 4 1/15. [3 marks: 1 for adding whole numbers and fractions separately; 1 for the common denominator 15; 1 for converting 3 16/15 to 4 1/15.] (Curriculum exemplar.)
(c) 5 − 2 3/4 = 4 4/4 − 2 3/4 = 2 1/4 (or 20/4 − 11/4 = 9/4 = 2 1/4). [2 marks]
(d) Fractions can only be added directly when their parts are the same size, i.e. when they have the same denominator; changing 1/2 and 1/3 to equivalents with a common denominator makes the parts equal in size. [1 mark. Accept any correct equivalent explanation.]
Question 4 — Word problems: addition and subtraction of fractions (B7.1.3.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 12 1/4 − 3 1/3 = 49/4 − 10/3 = 147/12 − 40/12 = 107/12 = 8 11/12 m. [3 marks: 1 for setting up the subtraction; 1 for the common-denominator work; 1 for the correct answer.] (Adapted curriculum exemplar.)
(b) 2 1/2 + 3 3/4 = 2 2/4 + 3 3/4 = 5 5/4 = 6 1/4 km. [3 marks]
(c) (i) 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12 [1]; (ii) 1 − 7/12 = 5/12 [1].
(d) 3/4 − 1/3 = 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12 litre. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Multiplying fractions; fraction of a quantity (B7.1.3.3.1 & B7.1.3.3.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 3 × 2 2/3 = 3 × 8/3 = 24/3 = 8 [2 marks: 1 for converting to an improper fraction, 1 for the answer] (curriculum exemplar); (ii) 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2 [2 marks].
(b) 2/3 × GH₵60.00 = GH₵40.00. [2 marks] (Curriculum exemplar.)
(c) 5/8 × 40 = 25 girls. [2 marks]
(d) 3/4 × 1,000 g = 750 g. [1 mark]
(e) 25% × 200 = 50. [1 mark]
Question 6 — Dividing fractions (B7.1.3.3.3 & B7.1.3.3.4)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 3/4 ÷ 3 = 3/4 × 1/3 = 3/12 = 1/4 [2 marks]; (ii) 1/2 ÷ 1/3 = 1/2 × 3/1 = 3/2 = 1 1/2 [2 marks].
(b) 10 ÷ 1/4 = 10 × 4 = 40 plates. [3 marks: 1 for setting up the division; 1 for multiplying by the reciprocal; 1 for the answer.] (Curriculum exemplar.)
(c) 15 ÷ 1 1/2 = 15 ÷ 3/2 = 15 × 2/3 = 10 bags. [2 marks]
(d) Dividing by 1/4 asks “how many quarters are in the number”, and there are 4 quarters in every whole, so the result is the same as multiplying by 4 (equivalently, multiplying by the reciprocal of 1/4). [1 mark. Accept any correct equivalent explanation.]
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically correct method unless the question specifies otherwise. Accept equivalent fractions that are correctly simplified.

Question 1 — Meaning of ratio and its relationship to fractions (B7.1.4.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 12 : 18 = 2 : 3 [1]; (ii) girls to all pupils: 18 : 30 = 3 : 5 [2 marks: 1 for 18 : 30, 1 for simplifying]; (iii) boys as a fraction: 12/30 = 2/5 [1].
(b) (i) 32 : 48 = 2 : 3 [1]; (ii) 25 : 75 : 50 = 1 : 3 : 2 [2 marks for fully correct; 1 mark for one error].
(c) 5 : 7 = □ : 35, so goats = (35 ÷ 7) × 5 = 25 goats. [2 marks: 1 for the scaling factor 5, 1 for the answer.]
(d) For every 3 of the first quantity there is 1 of the second quantity. [1 mark. Accept any correct equivalent wording.]
Question 2 — Unit rates (B7.1.4.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 3 : 4 [1]; (ii) 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar [2 marks: 1 for the division, 1 for the unit rate]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(b) 210 ÷ 3 = 70 km/h. [2 marks]
(c) GH₵27.00 ÷ 6 = GH₵4.50 per loaf. [2 marks]
(d) (i) GH₵180.00 ÷ 8 = GH₵22.50 per hour [2 marks]; (ii) GH₵22.50 × 5 = GH₵112.50 [1 mark].
Question 3 — Tables of equivalent ratios and sharing (B7.1.4.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 2/5 = 4/10 = 10/25 = 16/40. [1 mark per correct entry = 3 marks]
(b) Ages: 36 : 48 : 24 = 3 : 4 : 2. (i) 1 part = GH₵2,400.00 ÷ 2 = GH₵1,200.00 [1]; (ii) Kafui = 3 parts = GH₵3,600.00 [1]; (iii) Adoley = 4 parts = GH₵4,800.00 [1]; (iv) Total = 9 parts = GH₵10,800.00 [1]. (Adapted curriculum exemplar.)
(c) 3 + 4 = 7 parts; 1 part = GH₵560.00 ÷ 7 = GH₵80.00; shares are GH₵240.00 and GH₵320.00. [2 marks]
(d) Each ratio is obtained from 3 : 4 by multiplying both terms by the same number (×2 gives 6 : 8, ×3 gives 9 : 12), or each simplifies to 3 : 4. [1 mark. Accept any correct equivalent explanation.]
Question 4 — Proportional reasoning (B7.1.4.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) x = GH₵20.00 (since 6 is twice 3) [2 marks: 1 for the method, 1 for the value]; (ii) y = 12 (since GH₵40.00 is four times GH₵10.00) [1 mark]. (Curriculum exemplar structure.)
(b) (i) missing value = 12 [1]; (ii) Yes — the points lie on a straight line through the origin, and each second coordinate is 3 times the first (y = 3 × first number) [2 marks].
(c) (i) 45 ÷ 9 = 5 litres per minute [1]; (ii) 5 × 15 = 75 litres [1]; (iii) 120 ÷ 5 = 24 minutes [1].
(d) 4 : 9 = x : 36 ⇒ x = (4 × 36) ÷ 9 = 16. [1 mark]
Question 5 — Mixed applications  [10 marks]
(a) (i) water = 3 × 8 = 24 buckets [1]; (ii) mixture = 3 + 24 = 27 buckets [1].
(b) 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts; 1 part = GH₵450.00 ÷ 9 = GH₵50.00. (i) least share = GH₵100.00 [1]; (ii) greatest share = GH₵200.00 [1]; (iii) difference = GH₵200.00 − GH₵100.00 = GH₵100.00 [1].
(c) (i) Kofi: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 km/h; Ama: 240 ÷ 4 = 60 km/h [2 marks]; (ii) They are travelling at the same speed [1 mark].
(d) 4 : 6 simplifies to 2 : 3 (divide both terms by 2), or 2 : 3 becomes 4 : 6 by multiplying both terms by 2; multiplying or dividing both terms of a ratio by the same number does not change the relationship. [2 marks]
Question 6 — Creating and reasoning with ratios  [10 marks]
(a) Example: “In a basket, mangoes and oranges are in the ratio 3 : 5. If there are 15 mangoes, how many oranges are there?” Answer: 25 oranges. [3 marks: 1 for an appropriate real-life situation; 1 for the correct method; 1 for the correct answer.] Accept any sensible situation using 3 : 5.
(b) 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 parts; 1 part = 1,200 ÷ 12 = 100 books [1 mark]; JHS 1 = 300 books, JHS 2 = 400 books, JHS 3 = 500 books [3 marks: 1 per correct class share].
(c) (i) missing value = GH₵200.00 [1]; (ii) unit rate = GH₵50.00 ÷ 2 = GH₵25.00 per hour [1].
(d) Any two of: the graph is a straight line; the line passes through the origin (0, 0); the ratio of the y-value to the x-value is constant for every point. [1 mark for any two correct features.]
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically correct method unless the question specifies otherwise. Ratios should be given in their simplest form where required.

QUALITY-CONTROL SUMMARY
Check
Outcome
Curriculum scope
All 46 items trace to B7.1.4.1 (indicators .1–.4) only. No NaCCA indicators were invented; percentages as a topic, inverse proportion, scale drawing and gradient were excluded as out of scope. Coordinate-plane work kept to plotting/reading proportional pairs as the indicator allows.
Class appropriateness
JHS 1 (Basic 7) level: small whole-number ratios, unit rates from everyday contexts (transport, market, recipes, wages), sharing in given ratios including three-way sharing, and simple proportional tables.
BECE style
Section A uses 4-option MCQs with one defensible answer; Section B uses numbered parts with mark allocation and worked-response expectations, set in Ghanaian contexts (trotro, cedis, market sharing, farm animals).
Curriculum exemplars
Four curriculum exemplars are incorporated: the boys/girls 60 : 120 = 1 : 2 ratio (A1); the flour-to-sugar unit rate of 3/4 cup per cup (A11/B2a); the Kafui–Adoley–Jantuah age-ratio sharing with GH₵2,400 to the youngest (A22–A23/B3b); and the missing-value table 3 → 10, 6 → x, 9 → 30, y → 40 with x = 20, y = 12 (A30–A31/B4a).
Application & reasoning
38% of marks sit at Analyse/Create level; explanation items (B3d, B5d, B6d) and the create-a-situation item (B6a) carry the communication and reasoning demand.
MCQ distractors
All distractors model common learner errors: reversed ratios (A1-A, A6-B, A18-A), adding quantities (A28, A11-D), unsimplified ratios (A7-A), dividing the total by the number of people instead of parts (A20-C), and ratio-as-fraction confusion (A10-A).
Answer key verified
Every ratio simplification, unit rate, share and missing value was recomputed with exact arithmetic; all 46 keys confirmed correct.
Key balance & randomness
A = 11, B = 10, C = 9, D = 10; no consecutive correct letters repeat, so no answer pattern exists.
Marking consistency
Section A = 40 × 1 mark; Section B = 6 × 10 marks (each question’s parts verified to sum to 10); grand total 100 marks.
Language
Clear Ghanaian school English; BECE terminology used (“in its simplest form”, “unit rate”, “share in the ratio”, “equivalent ratios”); cedi sign GH₵ used throughout.
Originality
Except the curriculum exemplars noted above (public NaCCA materials), all items are original compositions for this mock; none is reproduced from WAEC/BECE past questions or any textbook.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Extending relations and patterns (B7.2.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 21, 25 [2 marks]; (ii) 162, 486 [2 marks]; (iii) 68, 60 [2 marks]. Award 1 mark per pair if one term of the pair is wrong.
(b) Each term is 4 more than the term before it (the common difference is +4). [1 mark]
(c) (i) Figure 4 uses 13 sticks [1]; (ii) each figure uses 3 more sticks than the one before it [1]; (iii) Figure 10 uses 4 + 9 × 3 = 31 sticks [1].
Question 2 — Describing rules in words and symbols (B7.2.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 2n + 1 [1]; (ii) 3n − 5 [1]; (iii) n/2 + 4 [1]; (iv) n² [1].
(b) (i) “One less than four times a number” [1]; (ii) “Twice the sum of a number and 3” [1]. Accept any correct equivalent wording.
(c) n = 1, 2, 3, 4 gives 3(1) − 2 = 1; 4; 7; 10 — the first four terms are 1, 4, 7, 10. [2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for one error.]
(d) Kwame’s rule describes how to move from one term to the next: 5 + 3 = 8, 8 + 3 = 11, 11 + 3 = 14 [1]. Ama’s rule gives each term from its position: 3 × 1 + 2 = 5, 3 × 2 + 2 = 8, 3 × 3 + 2 = 11, 3 × 4 + 2 = 14, so both generate the same sequence [1].
Question 3 — Identifying rules and making predictions (B7.2.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) y = 3x + 1 [2 marks: 1 for the multiplier 3, 1 for the +1]; (ii) 3 × 8 + 1 = 25 [1]; (iii) (40 − 1) ÷ 3 = 13 [1].
(b) 3 × 20 + 1 = 61 sticks. [2 marks]
(c) (i) 36 [1]; (ii) the terms are the square numbers: the nth term is n × n (n²) [1].
(d) (i) each term is multiplied by 3 [1]; (ii) 5th term = 162, so 6th term = 162 × 3 = 486 [1].
Question 4 — Tables of values and the number plane (B7.2.1.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) 2x + 1: −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, 7. [4 marks: 1 mark per correct pair of entries; minimum 0.] (Follows the curriculum exemplar: rule x → 2x + 1 on the domain {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3}.)
(b) (i) (−2, −3), (−1, −1), (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7) [1]; (ii) Yes, they lie on a straight line [1].
(c) P = (4, −3). [1 mark]
(d) For A(1, 3): 2 × 1 + 1 = 3, so A lies on the line; for B(2, 4): 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 ≠ 4, so B does not; for C(3, 7): 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, so C lies on the line. Points A and C lie on the graph. [2 marks]
(e) (0, 0). [1 mark]
Question 5 — Using relations to solve problems  [10 marks]
(a) (i) cost = 2 × number of pencils (y = 2x) [1]; (ii) 2 × 12 = GH₵24.00 [1]; (iii) 30 ÷ 2 = 15 pencils [1].
(b) (i) 5 + 3 × 4 = 17 cm [1]; (ii) 5 + 3w = 26 ⇒ 3w = 21 ⇒ w = 7 weeks [2 marks].
(c) (i) 4 + 2 × 10 = GH₵24.00 [1]; (ii) 4 + 2d = 36 ⇒ 2d = 32 ⇒ d = 16 km [2 marks].
(d) The fare increases by the same amount (GH₵2.00) for each extra kilometre, so the rate of change is constant, which always gives a straight-line graph. [1 mark. Accept any correct equivalent explanation.]
Question 6 — Creating patterns and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) Example: 2, 6, 10, … next two terms 14, 18. [3 marks: 1 for a correct starting pattern; 1 for a constant difference of 4; 1 for the correct next two terms.] Accept any correct pattern with common difference 4.
(b) Example: “At a fun fair, entry costs GH₵10.00 and each game costs GH₵5.00. The total cost of playing x games is y = 5x + 10.” When x = 6: y = 5 × 6 + 10 = GH₵40.00. [4 marks: 2 for an appropriate situation matching 5x + 10; 2 for the correct evaluation.]
(c) (i) The common difference is 4, and 4 × 1 − 1 = 3, so the nth term is 4n − 1 [2 marks]; (ii) 15th term = 4 × 15 − 1 = 59 [1 mark].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Accept any mathematically correct pattern, rule or situation unless the question specifies otherwise. Sequences should be extended exactly as the rule requires.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Translating word problems and equations (B7.2.3.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 2x − 7 = 41 [1]; (ii) 4x + x = 25 (accept 5x = 25) [1]; (iii) x + (x + 6) = 40 (accept 2x + 6 = 40) [1]. (These are the curriculum exemplars for B7.2.3.1.1, E.g.1 and E.g.2.)
(b) Any correct wording, e.g. (i) “the sum of two equal numbers is 15” [1]; (ii) “when 4 is taken away from 2 times a certain number, the result is 12” [1]; (iii) “two-thirds of a certain number is 4” [1]. (Curriculum exemplars E.g.3 i–iii.)
(c) (i) 2x − 7 = 41 ⇒ 2x = 48 ⇒ x = 24 [2 marks: 1 for the correct first step]; (ii) 2x − 4 = 12 ⇒ 2x = 16 ⇒ x = 8 [2 marks: 1 for the correct first step].
Question 2 — Modelling equations on a balance (B7.2.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) x + 3 = 10 [1]; (ii) remove the 3 kg weight from both sides / subtract 3 from both sides so the balance stays level [1]; (iii) x = 7 [1].
(b) 3x + 1 = x + 5; subtract x from both sides: 2x + 1 = 5 [1]; subtract 1 from both sides: 2x = 4 [1]; divide both sides by 2: x = 2 [1]; check: 3(2) + 1 = 7 = 2 + 5 [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(c) 3y + 4 = 2y + 8; subtract 2y from both sides: y + 4 = 8 [1]; subtract 4 from both sides: y = 4 [1]; check: 3(4) + 4 = 16 = 2(4) + 8 [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
Question 3 — Modelling equations with algebra tiles (B7.2.3.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) a rectangular tile represents x [1]; (ii) a small square unit tile represents 1 [1]; (iii) a zero pair is one positive tile and one negative tile of the same type, whose total value is 0 [1].
(b) Left side: 1 x-tile and 4 unit tiles; right side: 9 unit tiles [1]; remove 4 unit tiles from both sides (keeping the balance) [1]; leaves x = 5 [1].
(c) Model 2x + 3 = 9; remove 3 unit tiles from each side to get 2x = 6 [1]; share equally between the 2 x-tiles: x = 3 [1].
(d) Model 2x + 5 = x + 8; remove 1 x-tile from each side to get x + 5 = 8 [1]; remove 5 unit tiles from each side to get x = 3 [1].
Question 4 — Solving linear equations (B7.2.3.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) 3x + 5 = 20 ⇒ 3x + 5 − 5 = 20 − 5 ⇒ 3x = 15 [1] ⇒ x = 5 [1]. (Curriculum exemplar.)
(b) (i) 4x + 1 = 3x + 7 ⇒ x = 6 [2 marks]; (ii) 7w + 3 = 2w + 18 ⇒ 5w = 15 ⇒ w = 3 [2 marks]; (iii) 20 − 3k = k + 12 ⇒ 8 = 4k ⇒ k = 2 [2 marks]; (iv) 6z + 4 = 28 ⇒ 6z = 24 ⇒ z = 4 [2 marks]. (All four are curriculum exemplars for B7.2.3.1.4.) Award 1 mark only if the final value is right but steps are missing.
Question 5 — Solving problems with linear equations  [10 marks]
(a) (i) x − 5 = 12 [1]; (ii) x = 17 mangoes [1].
(b) (i) 3(x + 8) = 45 [2 marks; accept 3x + 24 = 45]; (ii) x + 8 = 15 ⇒ x = 7 [2 marks].
(c) (i) 2(w + 2w) = 30, i.e. 6w = 30 [2 marks; accept an equivalent unsimplified form]; (ii) w = 5 cm [2 marks].
Question 6 — Creating equations and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) Example: “A pen costs GH₵5.00 and Kwame pays GH₵3.00 for transport. He spends GH₵33.00 in all. How many pens did he buy?” Solve: 5x + 3 = 33 ⇒ 5x = 30 ⇒ x = 6 pens. [4 marks: 2 for an appropriate situation matching 5x + 3 = 33; 2 for the correct solution.] Accept any correct equivalent situation.
(b) x + x + x = 36, i.e. 3x = 36 [2 marks]; x = 12 [1 mark].
(c) Example: x + 5 = 9. Balance method: subtract 5 from both sides ⇒ x = 4. [3 marks: 2 for a correct equation with solution x = 4; 1 for showing the balance step.] Accept any correct equation whose solution is x = 4.
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. In every solved equation, accept any mathematically correct method (balance, inverse operations or tiles) provided the steps are shown. Word problems created by candidates must match the given equation exactly.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Measuring and classifying angles (B7.3.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) acute [1]; (ii) right [1]; (iii) obtuse [1]; (iv) reflex [1]; (v) straight [1].
(b) (i) greater than 0° and less than 90° [1]; (ii) greater than 180° and less than 360° [1].
(c) (i) Draw a straight base line; place the centre of the protractor on the end point of the line with the baseline of the protractor along the line; mark a point at the 60° graduation; remove the protractor and join the end point to the mark [2 marks for a complete, correctly ordered description]. (ii) Any two of 30°, 45°, 75°, 90°, 120°, 150°, 270°, 300° [1]. (The angle list follows the curriculum exemplar for B7.3.1.1.1, E.g.2.)
Question 2 — Complementary and supplementary angles (B7.3.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) two angles whose sum is 90° [1]; (ii) two angles whose sum is 180° [1]. (Curriculum definitions.)
(b) (i) 90° − 35° = 55° [1]; (ii) 90° − 62° = 28° [1]; (iii) 90° − 78° = 12° [1].
(c) (i) 180° − 110° = 70° [1]; (ii) 180° − 47° = 133° [1]; (iii) 180° − 90° = 90° [1].
(d) Let the angle be x°. Its complement is (90 − x)°, so x = (90 − x) + 20 ⇒ 2x = 110 ⇒ x = 55°. [2 marks: 1 for the equation, 1 for the value.]
Question 3 — Angles on straight lines and at a point (B7.3.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 180° − 70° = 110°. [2 marks]
(b) Angles on one side of a straight line sum to 180°: x = 180 − 45 − 60 = 75°. [2 marks]
(c) Angles at a point sum to 360°: x = 360 − 90 − 120 − 60 = 90°. [2 marks]
(d) x + (x + 40) = 180 [1] ⇒ 2x = 140 [1] ⇒ x = 70° [1]; the angles are 70° and 110° [1].
Question 4 — Vertically opposite angles (B7.3.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Vertically opposite angles are equal. [1 mark]
(b) (i) 65° [1]; (ii) 180° − 65° = 115° each [2 marks].
(c) Let the adjacent angles be y° and 3y°. y + 3y = 180 [1] ⇒ 4y = 180 [1] ⇒ y = 45° [1]; the four angles are 45°, 135°, 45° and 135° [1].
(d) 3x = x + 80 [1] ⇒ x = 40, and the angle is 3 × 40 = 120° [1].
Question 5 — Mixed angle problems  [10 marks]
(a) (i) complementary [1]; (ii) supplementary [1]; (iii) neither [1]; (iv) adjacent [1]. (Follows the curriculum exemplar B7.3.1.1.3, E.g.2.)
(b) Let the angle be x°. x = 2(90 − x) [1] ⇒ 3x = 180 [1] ⇒ x = 60° [1].
(c) x + 2x + 3x + 4x = 360 [1] ⇒ 10x = 360 ⇒ x = 36° [1]; the angles are 36°, 72°, 108° and 144° [1].
Question 6 — Drawing angles and reasoning  [10 marks]
(a) 45° drawn correctly with protractor [1]; 135° drawn correctly [1]; 45° + 135° = 180°, so they are supplementary [1].
(b) Example: complementary pair 40° and 50° since 40° + 50° = 90° [2]; supplementary pair 105° and 75° since 105° + 75° = 180° [2]. Accept any correct pairs with the sums shown.
(c) The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, i.e. 6° per minute [1]; in 20 minutes it turns 20 × 6 = 120° [1]; 120° is an obtuse angle [1].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Drawn angles may be accepted within ±2° of the required size. Accept any mathematically correct pair or method unless the question specifies otherwise.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Angle facts (B8.3.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) x + 115 = 180 (angles on a straight line) [1]; x = 65° [1].
(b) 120 + 85 + 90 + x = 360 (angles at a point) [1]; x = 65° [1].
(c) (i) Vertically opposite angle = 70° [1]; (ii) adjacent angle = 180° − 70° = 110° [2].
(d) Let the angle be x: x + 3x = 180 [1]; 4x = 180 [1]; x = 45° [1].
Question 2 — Transversals (B8.3.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Corresponding angle = 65°. [1 mark]
(b) Alternate angle = 65°. [1 mark]
(c) 180° − 65° = 115° [1]; co-interior angles are supplementary [1].
(d) The eight angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°. [3 marks — all eight correct.]
(e) Vertically opposite angles are equal, corresponding angles are equal, and angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so every angle must equal either 65° or 180° − 65° = 115°. [3 marks]
Question 3 — Angles in triangles (B8.3.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) ∠C = 180° − 50° − 60° = 70°. [2 marks]
(b) 2x + 3x + 4x = 180 [1]; 9x = 180, x = 20 [1]; angles are 40°, 60° and 80° [1].
(c) Third interior angle = 180° − 65° − 48° = 67°; exterior angle = 180° − 67° = 113° [2]; check: exterior angle = 65° + 48° = 113° ✓ [1].
(d) Base angles equal: ∠C = 68° [1]; ∠A = 180° − 68° − 68° = 44° [1].
Question 4 — Angles in polygons (B8.3.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°. [2 marks]
(b) (6 − 2) × 180° = 4 × 180° = 720°. [2 marks]
(c) 720° ÷ 6 = 120°. [2 marks]
(d) Exterior angle = 180° − 135° = 45° [2]; n = 360° ÷ 45° = 8 sides [2].
Question 5 — Applications (B8.3.1.1.1 / .2)  [10 marks]
(a) x + (x + 20) + (x + 40) = 180 [1]; 3x = 120, x = 40 [1]; angles 40°, 60°, 80° [1].
(b) 3k + 4k + 5k = 180 [1]; k = 15 [1]; angles 45°, 60°, 75° [1].
(c) n = 360° ÷ 36° = 10 sides [2]; interior angle = 180° − 36° = 144° [2].
Question 6 — Reasoning and deduction (B8.3.1.1.1 / .2)  [10 marks]
(a) Let the smaller angle be x: x + (x + 40) = 180 [1]; x = 70 [1]; angles 70° and 110° [1].
(b) (n − 2) × 180 = 1440 [1]; n − 2 = 8, n = 10 [1]; the polygon is a decagon [1].
(c) Interior : exterior = 4 : 1, and interior + exterior = 180° [1]; exterior = 180° ÷ 5 = 36° [1]; n = 360° ÷ 36° = 10 sides [2].
Note: Where the NaCCA curriculum exemplars reference diagrams (figures appear as images in the official PDF extract), fully text-based equivalents are used here; the angle relationships assessed are exactly those of the standard.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Construction of angles (B8.3.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Draw a ray AB. With centre A and any radius draw an arc cutting AB at P [1]. With the same radius and centre P, cut the arc at Q [1]. Join A to Q: ∠QAB = 60° [1].
(b) Continue stepping the same radius once more along the arc from Q to R [1]; join A to R: ∠RAB = 120° [1].
(c) Construct 120° as in (b), then bisect the angle between 120° and 180° [2]; alternatively construct 90° + 60° [1]. Result: 150° [1].
(d) Arcs of equal radius from the two points where the arms meet a construction arc, join A to their intersection [1]; each half = 60° [1].
Question 2 — More angle constructions (B8.3.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Construct 60° [1]; construct 90° [1]; bisect the angle between 90° and 120° to obtain 105° [1].
(b) Construct 90° [1]; bisect the angle between 90° and 180° to obtain 135° [1].
(c) 135° ÷ 2 = 67½°. [2 marks]
(d) Protractor [1]; compass constructions give exact values (no reading error) and can be reproduced precisely [2].
Question 3 — Construction of triangles (B8.3.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Draw VJ = 6.2 cm [1]. With centre V and radius 6.2 cm draw an arc; with centre J and the same radius draw an arc to meet it at N [1]. Join VN and JN: triangle VJN is equilateral [1].
(b) All three sides equal the same compass radius of 6.2 cm [1], so all three angles are 60° [1].
(c) Draw LM = 6 cm [1]. With centre L and radius 8 cm draw an arc; with centre M and radius 7 cm draw an arc to meet it at N [1]. Join LN and MN: triangle LMN is required [1].
(d) Scalene [1], because 6 cm, 7 cm and 8 cm are all different [1].
Question 4 — More triangle constructions (B8.3.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Draw the base 6 cm [1]; construct 50° at each end of the base [1]; extend the arms to meet at the vertex: the triangle is isosceles [1].
(b) Vertical angle = 180° − 50° − 50° = 80°. [2 marks]
(c) Construct ∠A = 45° [1]; mark AC = 3 cm and AB = 5 cm along the arms of the angle [1]; join B to C to complete triangle ABC [1].
(d) The sum of any two sides must be greater than the third side. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Loci (B8.3.1.2.3)  [10 marks]
(a) A circle with centre O and radius 5 cm. [2 marks]
(b) The perpendicular bisector of PQ. [2 marks]
(c) A circle (disc) of radius 4 m with the post as centre, shaded inside. [2 marks]
(d) With radius 10 m draw arcs from the flagpole and from the lamp post [2]; their intersections give the possible positions [1]; there are 2 possible positions [1].
Question 6 — Integrated loci (B8.3.1.2.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Construct the angle bisector of the angle between the paths [1]; draw a circle of radius 8 m with the intersection as centre [1]; the fountain is where the circle meets the bisector [1].
(b) A line midway between and parallel to both lines [2]; distance from each line = 5 cm [1].
(c) Draw two chords of the circle [1]; construct the perpendicular bisector of each chord [2]; their point of intersection is the centre, since the perpendicular bisector of every chord passes through the centre [1].
Note: In the official NaCCA extract, one exemplar angle (∠CAB in the two-sides-and-angle construction) appears with garbled notation (printed as 450); it is used here as 45°, the intended value, and all construction steps follow the methods described in the curriculum exemplars.

Question 1 — The circle (B8.3.2.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) C = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 14 = 88 cm. [2 marks]
(b) A = πr² = 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 616 cm². [2 marks]
(c) A = ½ × 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 77 cm². [2 marks]
(d) π(14² − 7²) = 22/7 × (196 − 49) = 22/7 × 147 = 462 cm². [2 marks]
(e) The sectors are arranged alternately to form an approximate rectangle [1]; its length ≈ πr and its width ≈ r, so A = πr × r = πr² [1].
Question 2 — The Pythagoras theorem (B8.3.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides: a² + b² = c². [2 marks]
(b) c² = 9 + 16 = 25 [1]; c = 5 cm [1].
(c) b² = 169 − 25 = 144 [1]; b = 12 cm [1].
(d) x² = 289 − 225 = 64 [1]; x = 8 cm [1].
(e) Area of square on side a + area of square on side b = area of square on the hypotenuse c [1]; so a² + b² = c² [1].
Question 3 — Pythagoras in real life (B8.3.2.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) d² = 2² + 9² = 85 [2]; d = √85 ≈ 9.2 m [1].
(b) The altitude bisects the base: half-base = 6 cm [1]; h² = 100 − 36 = 64 [1]; h = 8 cm [1].
(c) L² = 13² + 6² = 169 + 36 = 205 [2]; L = √205 ≈ 14.3 m [2].
Question 4 — Areas of triangles using Pythagoras (B8.3.2.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) h² = 12² − 6² = 108 [2]; h = √108 ≈ 10.4 cm [1].
(b) A = ½ × 12 × 10.39 ≈ 62.4 cm². [2 marks]
(c) P = 3 × 12 = 36 cm. [1 mark]
(d) (i) The string has two equal parts of 10 cm: length = 2 × 10 = 20 cm [2]; (ii) height = √(10² − 7.5²) = √43.75 ≈ 6.6 cm [1]; A = ½ × 15 × 6.6 ≈ 49.6 cm² [1].
Question 5 — Trigonometric ratios (B8.3.2.1.5)  [10 marks]
(a) sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse [1]; cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse [1]; tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent [1].
(b) sin θ = 3/5 [1]; cos θ = 4/5 [1]; tan θ = 3/4 [1].
(c) Angle of depression 30° means sin 30° = 18 ÷ d [1]; sin 30° = ½ [1]; d = 18 ÷ ½ = 36 m [2].
Question 6 — Integrated problems (B8.3.2.1.1 / .3)  [10 marks]
(a) πr² = 616 ⇒ r² = 616 × 7/22 = 196 [1]; r = 14 cm [1]; C = 2πr = 88 cm [1].
(b) Distance = one circumference = 88 cm. [1 mark]
(c) d² = 64 + 225 = 289 [1]; d = 17 m [1].
(d) Any sensible real-life Pythagoras problem [2]; correct working and answer [2].

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Vector concepts (B8.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) A vector is a quantity with both magnitude and direction [1]; (ii) a scalar is a quantity with magnitude only [1].
(b) 3 units to the right and 4 units up. [2 marks]
(c) (i) −p = (−2, 1) [1½ → award 1]; (ii) 3p = (6, −3) [2].
(d) AB goes from A to B while BA goes from B to A [1]; they have equal magnitudes but opposite directions [1], so AB = −BA [1].
Question 2 — Addition of vectors (B8.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) a + b = (2 + 4, 3 + 1) = (6, 4). [2 marks]
(b) AC = AB + BC = (3 + 1, 2 + 5) = (4, 7). [2 marks]
(c) PR = PQ + QR = (−2 + 5, 6 − 1) = (3, 5). [2 marks]
(d) a = (5 − 2, 4 + 3) = (3, 7). [2 marks]
(e) If two vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their sum is represented by the third side taken in the opposite order (AB + BC = AC). [2 marks]
Question 3 — Subtraction and scalar multiplication (B8.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) b − a = (3 + 2, −1 − 5) = (5, −6). [2 marks]
(b) −2q = (−6, −8). [2 marks]
(c) 2a = (4, 2); 3b = (3, −9) [1]; 2a − 3b = (4 − 3, 2 + 9) = (1, 11) [2].
(d) 4x = 12 ⇒ x = 3 [1½]; 4y = −8 ⇒ y = −2 [1½]; (x, y) = (3, −2).
Question 4 — Combined operations (B8.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 3q = (9, 12); 2p = (4, −2) [1]; 3q − 2p = (9 − 4, 12 + 2) = (5, 14) [2].
(b) 3p = (6, −3) [1]; r − 3p = (−2 − 6, 3 + 3) = (−8, 6) [2].
(c) q − p = (1, 5) [1]; 2r = (−4, 6) [1]; q − p + 2r = (1 − 4, 5 + 6) = (−3, 11) [2].
Question 5 — Vector equality (B8.3.2.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction (equal corresponding components). [2 marks]
(b) x = 7 [1]; y = 4 [1].
(c) 2x = 8 ⇒ x = 4 [1]; y = 3 [1]; x + y = 7 [1].
(d) x + 2 = 5 ⇒ x = 3 [1½]; y − 1 = 3 ⇒ y = 4 [1½].
Question 6 — Applications (B8.3.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Displacement = (3, 4) [1]; magnitude = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 km [2].
(b) (2 − 1, 5 + 3) = (1, 8) km. [2 marks]
(c) Second walk = (6 − 2, −2 − 3) = (4, −5). [2 marks]
(d) Any sensible two-journey vector problem [2]; correct addition and answer [1].
Note: Vectors are written in component form (x, y), representing x units horizontally and y units vertically, consistent with the NaCCA column-vector exemplars.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Rotation concepts (B8.3.3.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) A rotation is a transformation in which a shape turns through a given angle about a fixed point (the centre of rotation). [2 marks]
(b) The centre of rotation [1], the angle of rotation [1] and the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) [1].
(c) Any two, e.g. the blades of a turning fan, the hands of a clock, a steering wheel, a wheel of a bicycle. [2 marks]
(d) Clockwise is the direction in which the hands of a clock move [1]; anticlockwise is the opposite direction [1]; e.g. the clock hands move clockwise from 12 to 3 [1].
Question 2 — Rotation rules about the origin (B8.3.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) (x, y) → (−y, x) [1]; (ii) (x, y) → (−x, −y) [1]; (iii) (x, y) → (y, −x) [1].
(b) (2, 3) → (−3, 2). [2 marks]
(c) (4, −1) → (−1, −4). [2 marks]
(d) (−2, −5) → (2, 5). [1 mark]
(e) 270° anticlockwise = 90° clockwise: (−3, 4) → (4, 3). [2 marks]
Question 3 — Rotating a shape (B8.3.3.1.2 / .3)  [10 marks]
(a) A → (0, 1), B → (0, 3), C → (−2, 1). [3 marks — 1 per correct image.]
(b) A → (−1, 0), B → (−3, 0), C → (−1, −2). [3 marks — 1 per correct image.]
(c) The lengths of corresponding sides and the sizes of corresponding angles (the image is congruent to the object). [2 marks]
(d) C(1, 2) → (2, −1). [2 marks]
Question 4 — Angle of rotation (B8.3.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 90° [1], clockwise [1].
(b) 8 × 30° = 240°. [2 marks]
(c) 3 × 90° = 270°. [2 marks]
(d) Compare (2, 7) with (−7, 2): this matches (x, y) → (−y, x) [2]; the rotation is 90° anticlockwise about the origin [2].
Question 5 — Congruence (B8.3.3.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Congruent shapes have exactly the same shape and the same size. [2 marks]
(b) A rotation only turns the shape about the centre [1]; it does not change any side length [1] or any angle [1], so object and image are congruent.
(c) P′Q′ = 5 cm [1]; ∠P′ = 40° [1].
(d) XYZ: XY = 4, XZ = 3, YZ = √(4² + 3²) = 5 [1]. Images: X′(0, 0), Y′(0, 4), Z′(−3, 0) [1]; X′Y′ = 4, X′Z′ = 3, Y′Z′ = 5 — the sides are equal, so the triangles are congruent [1].
Question 6 — Integrated problems (B8.3.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (3, −2) → (−3, 2) is (x, y) → (−x, −y) [1]: a rotation of 180° about the origin [1].
(b) (3, 0) → (0, −3) [1]: 270° anticlockwise (equivalently 90° clockwise) about the origin [1].
(c) 540° ÷ 360° = 1½ turns. [2 marks]
(d) Any point with a valid rotation about the origin [2]; correct image using the appropriate rule [2].

Curriculum scope

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Types of data (B8.4.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) Discrete data are counts which take separate (whole-number) values [1]; (ii) continuous data are measurements which can take any value within a range [1].
(b) (i) discrete [1]; (ii) continuous [1]; (iii) discrete [1]; (iv) continuous [1].
(c) Any two, e.g. sex (male/female), marital status, income group, movie type. [2 marks]
(d) Raw data are facts and figures collected directly, before being organised [1]; e.g. the scores of learners in a test as collected [1].
Question 2 — Methods of data collection (B8.4.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Any two: questionnaire/survey, interview, observation, experiment, measurement, records. [2 marks]
(b) An experiment [1]: the amount of crackers eaten is deliberately changed [1] and the effect on productivity is measured under controlled conditions [1].
(c) Any sensible two-question form, e.g. ‘How many hours do you study per day?’ and ‘Where do you study?’ with response spaces. [3 marks — 1 for each usable question plus layout.]
(d) Any one: many people can be reached quickly; answers are easy to compare/tally; respondents answer privately. [2 marks]
Question 3 — Frequency tables (B8.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Frequencies: 25–29: 2; 30–34: 4; 35–39: 7; 40–44: 9; 45–49: 8; 50–54: 7; 55–59: 3. [5 marks — 1 per correct row, total must be 40.]
(b) Modal class: 40–44 (frequency 9). [1 mark]
(c) 50–54 and 55–59: 7 + 3 = 10 leaves. [2 marks]
(d) Class width = 5 mm. [2 marks]
Question 4 — Bar charts and pie charts (B8.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 120 + 80 + 40 + 110 + 50 = GH₵400.00. [1 mark]
(b) Food: 120/400 × 360° = 108°; Rent: 80/400 × 360° = 72°; Clothing: 40/400 × 360° = 36°; Transport: 110/400 × 360° = 99°; Savings: 50/400 × 360° = 45°. [4 marks — 1 per correct angle, rounding allowed.]
(c) Bar chart: correct scale and labels, bars of heights 120, 80, 40, 110, 50. [3 marks]
(d) Pie chart: circle divided according to the angles in (b), sectors labelled. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Stem-and-leaf plots, waffle charts and pictograms (B8.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Stem | Leaf:  2 | 5 6 9;  3 | 0 5 7;  4 | 0 5 5 7;  5 | 0  (with key, e.g. 2 | 5 means 25). [4 marks — 1 per correct stem row.]
(b) 64 cells are shaded [1]; each cell represents 1% (one percentage point) [1].
(c) 35 ÷ 5 = 7 symbols. [2 marks]
(d) Leaving the row blank shows clearly that no data value falls in that interval [1]; writing 0 would suggest a score of 0 was recorded in that stem [1].
Question 6 — Integrated problems (B8.4.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Frequency table: mango 12, orange 8, banana 6, pawpaw 4; total 30. [2 marks]
(b) Mango: 12/30 × 360° = 144°; Orange: 8/30 × 360° = 96°; Banana: 6/30 × 360° = 72°; Pawpaw: 4/30 × 360° = 48°. [4 marks]
(c) Modal fruit: mango [1]; fraction = 12/30 = 2/5 [1].
(d) Any eight numbers grouped into two correct classes with correct frequencies. [2 marks]
Note: The leaf-length data set, the cleaner’s expenditure and the waffle-chart context follow the NaCCA curriculum exemplars; all computations were verified.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — The mean (B8.4.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (4 + 7 + 9 + 12) ÷ 4 = 32 ÷ 4 = 8. [2 marks]
(b) Sum = 5 × 12 = 60. [2 marks]
(c) (x + 5 + 7 + 10) ÷ 4 = 7 [1]; x + 22 = 28 [1]; x = 6 [1].
(d) 70 ÷ 5 = 14. [2 marks]
(e) 5 × 142 − 4 × 140 = 710 − 560 = 150 cm. [1 mark]
Question 2 — Median, mode and range (B8.4.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Ordered: 1, 4, 5, 7, 9 [1]; median = 5 [1].
(b) Median = (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7. [2 marks]
(c) 3 (it occurs most often, three times). [2 marks]
(d) 2 and 4 (both occur twice): the data are bimodal. [2 marks]
(e) Range = 11 − 2 = 9. [2 marks]
Question 3 — The house-area data (B8.4.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Mean = 210 ÷ 7 = 30 m². [2 marks]
(b) Ordered: 22, 24, 26, 30, 30, 30, 48 [1]; median = 30 m² [1].
(c) Mode = 30 m² (occurs three times). [2 marks]
(d) Range = 48 − 22 = 26 m². [1 mark]
(e) The values below 30 (22, 24, 26) balance the high value 48 above 30 [2]; the data are centred on 30, so all three measures give 30 [1].
Question 4 — Kojo’s taxi trips (B8.4.1.2.1 / .2)  [10 marks]
(a) Mean = 56 ÷ 7 = 8 trips. [2 marks]
(b) Ordered: 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10 [1]; median = 9 trips [1].
(c) Mode = 10 trips. [2 marks]
(d) The median [1]: it is not pulled down by the low Sunday value of 3, so it best describes a typical day [2]; the mean (8) is dragged down by the outlier while the mode (10) is the maximum value and overstates a typical day [1].
Question 5 — A frequency table (B8.4.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 1 + 11 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 25 values. [1 mark]
(b) Total = 1(1) + 2(11) + 3(5) + 4(4) + 5(2) + 6(1) + 7(1) = 77 [2]; mean = 77 ÷ 25 = 3.08 [1].
(c) The median is the 13th value [1]; cumulative frequencies: 1, 12, 17, … so the 13th value lies at data value 3 [2].
(d) Mode = 2 (frequency 11). [1 mark]
(e) The data are skewed: most values are small (eleven 2s), pulling the mode down to 2, while the few larger values pull the mean up to 3.08 [2].
Question 6 — Choosing and creating (B8.4.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) The mode [1]: the shop needs the size that occurs most often [1].
(b) The median [1]: the manager’s very high salary is an outlier that would pull the mean up [1]; the median gives a typical worker’s salary [1].
(c) When all the values are important and there are no extreme values/outliers [2].
(d) Any valid set, e.g. 2, 3, 3, 3, 4 [1]: mean = 15 ÷ 5 = 3, median = 3, mode = 3 [2].
