Question 1 — Sample spaces (B8.4.2.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of a probability experiment. [2 marks]
(b) (i) {H, T} [1]; (ii) {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} [1].
(c) {HH, HT, TH, TT}. [2 marks]
(d) 6 × 2 = 12 outcomes. [2 marks]
(e) The outcome of one event does not affect the outcome of the other [1]; e.g. tossing a coin and throwing a die [1].
Question 2 — The bottle-top experiment (B8.4.2.1.1 / .2)  [10 marks]
(a) P(red) = 3/6 = 1/2. [2 marks]
(b) (i) P(green) = 2/6 = 1/3 [1]; (ii) P(pink) = 1/6 [1].
(c) P(not red) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. [2 marks]
(d) (i) 0.5 [1→]; (ii) 50% [1]; (iii) 1 : 2 (or 3 : 6) [1]. Total for (d) = 4: 1 for the decimal, 1 for the percentage, 2 for the ratio as favourable : total.
Question 3 — The pen experiment (B8.4.2.1.1 / .2)  [10 marks]
(a) {BB, BP, PB, PP}. [2 marks]
(b) Tree diagram: first draw branches 3/7 (blue), 4/7 (pink); each second-draw branch again 3/7 and 4/7; four final outcomes BB, BP, PB, PP. [4 marks — structure 2, branch probabilities 2.]
(c) P(BB) = 3/7 × 3/7 = 9/49. [2 marks]
(d) P(one of each) = P(BP) + P(PB) = 12/49 + 12/49 = 24/49. [2 marks]
Question 4 — The spinner experiment (B8.4.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) {WW, WL, LW, LL}. [2 marks]
(b) P(W) = 1/2 [1]; P(L) = 1/2 [1].
(c) P(WW) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 [1½]; P(LL) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 [1½].
(d) (i) 0.5 [1]; (ii) 50% [1]; (iii) 1 : 2 [1].
Question 5 — Conversions (B8.4.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5. [2 marks]
(b) 45% = 45/100 = 9/20. [2 marks]
(c) 3/8 = 0.375. [2 marks]
(d) P(loss) = 1 − 3/5 = 2/5 [2]; 2/5 = 40% [2].
Question 6 — Integrated problems (B8.4.2.1.1 / .2)  [10 marks]
(a) P(stops at first throw) = 1/6. [2 marks]
(b) P(no 6 then 6) = 5/6 × 1/6 = 5/36. [3 marks]
(c) The game stops as soon as a 6 is scored [1], so no further throws occur after a 6 and those branches disappear [1].
(d) Any valid two-event experiment with replacement or independent trials [1]; correct sample space [1]; correct probability [1].

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Reading, writing and place value (B8.1.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Four billion, fifty-six million, seven thousand and ninety. [2 marks]
(b) 6,203,040,015. [2 marks]
(c) (i) 8 [1]; (ii) The digit 7 is in the ten millions place, so its place value is 70,000,000 [2].
(d) Two million, four hundred and fifty-six thousand, seven hundred and eighty-nine [2]; the digit 5 is in the ten thousands place, so its place value is 50,000 [1].
Question 2 — Skip counting (B8.1.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 200,000; 700,000; 1,200,000; 1,700,000; 2,200,000. [4 marks — award 1 for each correct number after the start.]
(b) 1,800,000; 1,699,950; 1,599,900. [3 marks — 1 for each correct number.]
(c) 250,000 → 300,000 → 350,000 → 400,000 → 450,000, so after 4 months the scheme holds GH₵450,000. [3 marks]
Question 3 — Comparing and ordering (B8.1.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 3,450,000,000 > 3,405,000,000 [1]; (ii) 2,090,000,000 = 2,090,000,000 [1].
(b) 5,006,000,000; 5,060,000,000; 5,600,000,000. [3 marks]
(c) (i) Town B (1,295,800,000) [2]; (ii) 1,295,800,000 − 1,295,300,000 = 500,000 [3 marks — 1 for the method, 2 for the answer].
Question 4 — Standard form (B8.1.1.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 375 = 3.75 × 10² [2]; (ii) 8,650,049 = 8.650049 × 10⁶ [2]; (iii) 26 = 2.6 × 10 [2].
(b) (i) 4.2 × 10⁵ = 420,000 [2]; (ii) 1.06 × 10⁷ = 10,600,000 [2].
Question 5 — Significant figures and decimal places (B8.1.1.1.5)  [10 marks]
(a) The significant figures of a number are the digits that carry meaning about its size, counted from the first non-zero digit; leading zeros are not significant. [2 marks]
(b) (i) 57,000 [2]; (ii) 56,700 [2].
(c) (i) 975.87 [1]; (ii) 975.867 [1]; (iii) 975.9 [2].
Question 6 — Real-life problems (B8.1.1.1.6)  [10 marks]
(a) Arko earns 3 × 2,500 = GH₵7,500 a month [1]; together 2,500 + 7,500 = GH₵10,000 a month [1]; in a year 10,000 × 12 = GH₵120,000 [1]; in five years 120,000 × 5 = GH₵600,000 [1].
(b) 615 × 1,000 = 615,000 km [2]; in standard form 6.15 × 10⁵ km [1].
(c) Any sensible word problem using place value of a number above one billion [2]; correct solution [1].
Note: Award no marks merely for copying the question. Numbers must be written with correct place-value grouping, and standard form must be given as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Sets of factors and common factors (B8.1.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 42: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21 and 42. [2 marks — 1 for listing correctly, 1 for completeness.]
(b) 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36. [2 marks]
(c) Common factors: {1, 2, 3, 6}. [2 marks — 1 for method (comparing lists), 1 for correct set.]
(d) HCF = 6. [2 marks]
(e) Common factors of 24 and 32: {1, 2, 4, 8} [1]; HCF = 8 [1].
Question 2 — Perfect squares (B8.1.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) A perfect square is a number whose square root is a whole number (i.e. the product of a whole number multiplied by itself). [2 marks]
(b) Listing multiples of 5 up to 50, only 25 = 5 × 5 is a perfect square. [2 marks]
(c) 64, 81, 100, 121, 144 and 169 (i.e. 8² to 13²). [3 marks — 1 for each two correct.]
(d) Side = √2,025 = 45 m. [3 marks — 1 for recognising side = √area, 2 for 45 m.]
Question 3 — Square roots (B8.1.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 49 − 1 = 48; 48 − 3 = 45; 45 − 5 = 40; 40 − 7 = 33; 33 − 9 = 24; 24 − 11 = 13; 13 − 13 = 0. Seven odd numbers were subtracted, so √49 = 7. [4 marks — 2 for the odd-subtraction steps, 1 for reaching zero, 1 for √49 = 7.]
(b) 576 = 24 × 24, so √576 = 24. (Award full marks for prime factorisation: 576 = 2⁶ × 3², √576 = 2³ × 3 = 24.) [3 marks]
(c) √(196 × 225) = √196 × √225 = 14 × 15 = 210. [3 marks — 1 for splitting, 2 for 210.]
Question 4 — Union and intersection of sets (B8.1.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) A ∩ B = {4, 5}. [2 marks]
(b) A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. [2 marks]
(c) Elements not in A ∪ B: {9, 10}. [2 marks]
(d) n(A ∪ B) = 20 + 25 − 10 = 35. [2 marks]
(e) n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). [2 marks]
Question 5 — Venn diagram problem (B8.1.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Two overlapping circles labelled Maize and Rice inside a universal set (80). Regions: Maize only = 50 − x, intersection = x, Rice only = 60 − x. [3 marks — 1 for correct diagram, 2 for correct region labels.]
(b) (50 − x) + x + (60 − x) = 80 ⇒ 110 − x = 80 ⇒ x = 30. [4 marks — 2 for equation, 2 for solution.]
(c) (i) Maize only = 50 − 30 = 20 farmers [1½]; (ii) Rice only = 60 − 30 = 30 farmers [1½].
Question 6 — Applied set problems (B8.1.1.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 38 + 32 − x = 60 ⇒ x = 10 students take both languages. [3 marks — 1 for equation, 2 for x = 10.]
(b) Twi only = 32 − 10 = 22 students. [2 marks]
(c) All 15 new students take both languages, so n(F ∪ T) increases by 15: 60 + 15 = 75. [2 marks]
(d) Any sensible real-life problem using the intersection of two sets [2]; correct solution [1].
Note: In set questions, repeated elements must be counted once in a union; award no marks where elements of the intersection are double-counted.

Question 1 — Powers of 10 and benchmark fractions (B8.1.2.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 345 [1]; (ii) 78 [1]; (iii) 62.5 [1]; (iv) 0.96 [1].
(b) (i) ¼ = 0.25 [1]; (ii) ¾ = 0.75 [1].
(c) (i) 0.6 = 3/5 [1]; (ii) 60% [1].
(d) 12.5% = 0.125. [2 marks]
Question 2 — Mental mathematics strategies (B8.1.2.1.2, B8.1.2.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Halve 24 and double 35: 24 × 35 = 12 × 70 = 840. [3 marks — 1 for the transformation, 2 for 840.]
(b) (i) 70 × 80 = 5,600 [1]; (ii) 700 × 80 = 56,000 [1].
(c) 25 = 100 ÷ 4, so 56 × 25 = (56 ÷ 4) × 100 = 14 × 100 = 1,400. [3 marks — 1 for the strategy, 2 for 1,400.]
(d) 15 × 24 = 30 × 12 = 360 seedlings. [2 marks — 1 for answer, 1 for a valid mental strategy.]
Question 3 — Addition and subtraction (B8.1.2.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 896,854 = 800,000 + 90,000 + 6,000 + 800 + 50 + 4; 76,329 = 70,000 + 6,000 + 300 + 20 + 9. Adding place by place: 800,000 + 70,000 + 90,000 + 6,000 + 6,000 + 800 + 300 + 50 + 20 + 4 + 9 = 973,183. [4 marks — 2 for the expansions, 2 for the correct total.]
(b) 3,627.6 + 854.13 = 4,481.73. [2 marks]
(c) 193.6 − 37.85 = 155.75. [2 marks]
(d) 45,678 + 12,345 = 58,023; 100,000 − 58,023 = 41,977. [2 marks]
Question 4 — Multiplication and division (B8.1.2.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 657 × 7 = 4,599; 657 × 20 = 13,140; 4,599 + 13,140 = 17,739. [3 marks — 1 for each partial product and the total.]
(b) 325 × 15 = 325 × (10 + 5) = 3,250 + 1,625 = 4,875. [3 marks — 1 for the split, 2 for 4,875.]
(c) 12,096 ÷ 24 = 504. [2 marks]
(d) 10,000 = 32 × 312 + 16, so quotient = 312, remainder = 16. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Divisibility tests (B8.1.2.2.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 [1]; (ii) similarly for 9 — the sum of the digits must be divisible by 9 [1].
(b) 5,346: 5 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 18, and 18 is divisible by 9, so 5,346 is divisible by 9. (The other digit sums are 16, 16 and 17, none divisible by 9.) [2 marks]
(c) Last three digits 312 ÷ 8 = 39, so 4,312 is divisible by 8; quotient 4,312 ÷ 8 = 539. [3 marks — 1 for the test, 2 for the quotient.]
(d) The units digit of 5,346 is 6; the next multiple of 5 ends in 0, i.e. 5,350, so add 5,350 − 5,346 = 4. [3 marks — 1 for reasoning, 2 for the answer.]
Question 6 — Story problems (B8.1.2.2.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Kofi: 8 × 12.00 = GH₵96.00; Ama: 12 × 5.00 = GH₵60.00; total = GH₵156.00. [3 marks — 1 for each product, 1 for the total.]
(b) 2,477.25 ÷ 3 = GH₵825.75. [3 marks]
(c) 25.25 ÷ 5 = 5.05 m. [2 marks]
(d) Any sensible story problem multiplying a decimal by a whole number [1]; correct solution [1].

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — The laws of indices (B8.1.2.3.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Law 1: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ [1]; Law 2: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ [1]; Law 3: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ [1].
(b) Law 4: (ab)ⁿ = aⁿ bⁿ. [1 mark]
(c) Take m = n = 1 in Law 2: a¹ ÷ a¹ = a¹⁻¹ = a⁰ [2]; but a¹ ÷ a¹ = 1, so a⁰ = 1 [1].
(d) 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 4⁵ [1]; base = 4 (the repeated factor) [1]; index = 5 (the number of times the base is used as a factor) [1].
Question 2 — Evaluating powers (B8.1.2.3.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 2⁵ × 2³ = 2⁸ = 256. [2 marks]
(b) (5²)³ = 5⁶ = 15,625. [2 marks]
(c) (2 × 3)⁴ = 6⁴ = 1,296. [2 marks]
(d) 5 × 16² = 5 × 256 = 1,280 (PEDMAS: index before multiplication). [2 marks]
(e) (16/81)⁻³/⁴: invert to remove the negative index → (81/16)³/⁴; fourth root of 81/16 is 3/2; (3/2)³ = 27/8. [2 marks — 1 for handling the negative index, 1 for 27/8.]
Question 3 — Exponential equations (B8.1.2.3.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 25 = 5², so 5² = 5²ˣ; equating indices: 2 = 2x, x = 1. [2 marks]
(b) 16 = 2⁴, so x + 2 = 4, x = 2. [2 marks]
(c) 2⁵/2³ = 2² [1]; hence 2² = 2²ˣ [1]; x = 1 [1].
(d) 1/27 = 3⁻³ [2]; hence x = −3 [1].
Question 4 — Simplifying with the laws of indices (B8.1.2.3.2)  [10 marks]
(a) 3²⁺⁵⁻⁴ = 3³ = 27. [2 marks]
(b) 2⁶ × 2⁴ = 2¹⁰ = 1,024. [2 marks]
(c) a³⁻⁵ = a⁻² = 1/a². [2 marks]
(d) 4² = (2²)² = 2⁴ [1]; so (2³ × 2⁴) ÷ 2⁵ = 2² = 4 [1].
(e) 27/32 = 3³/2⁵. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Saratu’s ancestors (B8.1.2.3.4)  [10 marks]
Generation 1: 2, Generation 2: 4, Generation 3: 8, Generation 4: 16, Generation 5: 32. [3 marks — 1 for each correct pair after the first entry.]
(b) Number of ancestors in generation n = 2ⁿ. [2 marks]
(c) 2¹² = 4,096 ancestors. [2 marks]
(d) Total = 2 + 4 + 8 + … + 4,096 = 2(2¹² − 1) = 8,190. [3 marks — 1 for setting up the sum, 2 for 8,190.]
Question 6 — Real-life applications (B8.1.2.3.4)  [10 marks]
(a) 2⁶ = 64 bacteria. [3 marks — 1 for recognising powers of 2, 2 for 64.]
(b) GH₵50 × 2³ = GH₵50 × 8 = GH₵400. [3 marks — 1 for the power, 2 for GH₵400.]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Review of fractions (B8.1.3.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Any three of 4/6, 6/9, 8/12, 10/15, … (any fraction kn/3n). [3 marks — 1 for each correct equivalent fraction.]
(b) 6/10 = 3/5. [2 marks]
(c) 12/5 = 2 2/5. [2 marks]
(d) 2 5/9 = (2 × 9 + 5)/9 = 23/9. [3 marks — 1 for the method, 2 for 23/9.]
Question 2 — Operations on fractions (B8.1.3.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 3/4 + 7/8 = 6/8 + 7/8 = 13/8 = 1 5/8. [2 marks]
(b) 4/5 − 1/6 = 24/30 − 5/30 = 19/30. [2 marks]
(c) 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2. [2 marks]
(d) 5/8 ÷ 2 1/2 = 5/8 ÷ 5/2 = 5/8 × 2/5 = 10/40 = 1/4. [2 marks]
(e) 1 1/2 + 2 3/4 = 6/4 + 11/4 = 17/4 = 4 1/4. [2 marks]
Question 3 — Order of operations (B8.1.3.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) Multiply first: 5/8 × 4/5 = 1/2 [1]; then 3/4 + 1/2 − 1/6 = 9/12 + 6/12 − 2/12 = 13/12 = 1 1/12 [2].
(b) 3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 3/4 × 8/3 = 2 [1]; 4/5 − 1/2 = 3/10 [1]; 2 + 3/10 = 2 3/10 [2].
(c) 3/4 + 5/8 = 11/8 [1]; 11/8 × 4/11 = 1/2 [1]; 1/2 − 1/2 = 0 [1].
Question 4 — Fractions of quantities (B8.1.3.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 2/3 × 240 = GH₵160.00 [2]; (ii) 240 − 160 = GH₵80.00 [1].
(b) 42/60 = 7/10 = 70%. [3 marks — 1 for the fraction, 2 for 70%.]
(c) 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12 [2]; fraction going home = 1 − 11/12 = 1/12 [2].
Question 5 — Measurement with fractions (B8.1.3.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) Perimeter = 2(1 1/3 + 3 3/4) = 2(4/3 + 15/4) = 2(16/12 + 45/12) = 2 × 61/12 = 61/6 = 10 1/6 cm. [5 marks — 2 for converting to improper fractions, 2 for the addition, 1 for 10 1/6 cm.]
(b) Area = 4/3 × 15/4 = 60/12 = 5 cm². [3 marks]
(c) 2/7 = 8/28 and 1/4 = 7/28; since 8/28 > 7/28, Esi’s drink tastes stronger. [2 marks]
Question 6 — Integrated problems (B8.1.3.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 1/4 × 240 = 60; 1/3 × 240 = 80; total = 140 pages. [3 marks — 1 for each fraction, 1 for the total.]
(b) 240 − 140 = 100 pages. [2 marks]
(c) 140/240 = 7/12 = 0.5833… ≈ 0.58. [3 marks — 2 for 7/12, 1 for 0.58 to 2 d.p.]
(d) Any sensible word problem using division of fractions [1]; correct solution [1].
Note: Fraction answers must be given in their simplest form unless otherwise stated. In BODMAS questions, marks for method require the correct order of operations to be shown.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — Unit conversion by ratio reasoning (B8.1.4.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) 3,500 m [1]; (ii) 4.5 m [1]; (iii) 2,250 mL [1]; (iv) 135 minutes [1].
(b) Since 1 m = 100 cm, the ratio 100 cm/1 m equals 1 [1]; multiplying by it changes the unit but not the size of the measurement [1]; the metres cancel and centimetres remain [1].
(c) Agbo: 4 km in 1 h = 4 km/h [1]; Rukiya: 4.2 km in 0.75 h = 5.6 km/h [1]; Rukiya is faster [1].
Question 2 — Unit rate problems (B8.1.4.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) (i) Rate = 4 lawns in 7 h = 4/7 of a lawn per hour [2]; (ii) in 35 h: 35 × 4/7 = 20 lawns [2].
(b) 756 ÷ 3 = 252 calories per hour. [3 marks — 1 for the ratio 756 : 3, 2 for 252.]
(c) (i) 42 ÷ 6 = GH₵7.00 [2]; (ii) 10 × 7 = GH₵70.00 [1].
Question 3 — Speed and distance–time graphs (B8.1.4.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 8 miles in 1 hour = 8 miles/h. [2 marks]
(b) Remaining distance = 20 − 8 = 12 miles [1]; 24 min = 0.4 h [1]; speed = 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 miles/h [1].
(c) Distance axis 0–20 miles, time axis 0–168 min. Straight line from (0, 0) to (60, 8) [1]; horizontal section from (60, 8) to (96, 8) [1]; straight line from (96, 8) to (120, 20), with return optional to (168, 0) as described [1].
(d) The object is at rest (distance is not changing). [2 marks]
Question 4 — Proportional relationships (B8.1.4.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) Two quantities are proportional if their ratio is constant (equivalently, one is a constant multiple of the other, so the graph is a straight line through the origin). [2 marks]
(b) y/x = 6/1 = 12/2 = 18/3 = 24/4 = 6; the ratios are equivalent, so the relationship is proportional. [3 marks — 2 for the ratios, 1 for the conclusion.]
(c) y/x = 6/1, 11/2, 16/3, 21/4 — the ratios are not equivalent, so the relationship is NOT proportional. [3 marks — 2 for the ratios, 1 for the conclusion.]
(d) A proportional relationship gives a straight line through the origin; a non-proportional linear relationship gives a straight line which does not pass through the origin. [2 marks]
Question 5 — Constant of proportionality (B8.1.4.1.5)  [10 marks]
(a) k = (9/8) ÷ 45 = 9/360 = 1/40 of an inch per second. [4 marks — 2 for setting up the division, 2 for 1/40.]
(b) 2 min 15 s = 135 s [1]; k = (27/8) ÷ 135 = 27/1080 = 1/40 [1]; same constant, so the relationship is proportional [1].
(c) k = y/x = 36/4 = 9 [2]; equation: y = 9x [1].
Question 6 — Integrated problems (B8.1.4.1.1/.2/.5)  [10 marks]
(a) 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h. [2 marks]
(b) 400 ÷ 80 = 5 hours. [3 marks — 1 for the method, 2 for 5 hours.]
(c) k = 60 ÷ 5 = GH₵12.00 per kg [2]; 8 kg costs 8 × 12 = GH₵96.00 [1].
(d) Any sensible unit-rate problem from real life [1]; correct solution [1].
Note: In rate questions, units must be converted before dividing (e.g. minutes to hours). Graph questions require correctly labelled axes and key points.

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME (60 marks)
Question 1 — The gradient of a straight line (B8.2.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) Gradient = Δy/Δx = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). [2 marks]
(b) m = (2 − 1)/(7 − 1) = 1/6. [2 marks]
(c) m = (4 − (−2))/(−3 − 3) = 6/−6 = −1. [3 marks — 1 for substitution, 2 for −1.]
(d) 2x − 8y + 3 = 0 ⇒ 8y = 2x + 3 ⇒ y = (1/4)x + 3/8, so m = 1/4. [3 marks — 2 for rearranging, 1 for 1/4.]
Question 2 — Equations of straight lines (B8.2.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) y = 2x − 3 [2]; when x = 4: y = 2(4) − 3 = 5 [2].
(b) y = (−5/2)x + 7/2. [2 marks]
(c) m = (−2 − 4)/(−10 − 5) = −6/−15 = 2/5 [2]; c = 4 − (2/5)(5) = 2 [1]; equation: y = (2/5)x + 2 [1].
Question 3 — Point-slope form and rearranging (B8.2.1.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) y − (−1) = (2/3)(x − 3) [2]; y + 1 = (2/3)x − 2 ⇒ y = (2/3)x − 3 [2].
(b) 4y = −5x + 3 ⇒ y = (−5/4)x + 3/4 [2]; gradient = −5/4, y-intercept = 3/4 [2].
(c) m = (5 − 4)/(3 − (−2)) = 1/5. [2 marks]
Question 4 — Tables of values and graphs (B8.2.1.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) x: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → y: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. [3 marks — ½ for each correct pair.]
(b) Correct axes and scale [1]; accurate plotting of at least five points [1]; straight line through the origin [1].
(c) (i) Cost of 3.5 kg = GH₵70 [2]; (ii) GH₵80 buys 4 kg [2]. (Accept values read correctly from the graph.)
Question 5 — Real-life linear graphs (B8.2.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) h: 0, 3, 6 → d: 0, 1, 2 [3]; after 6 hours the distance is 2 km [1].
(b) (i) 3 × 50 = GH₵150 [2]; (ii) 175 ÷ 50 = 3½ hours [2]; (iii) 300 ÷ 50 = 6 hours [2].
Question 6 — The Wawa tree (B8.2.1.1.2 / B8.2.1.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) x: 0, 10, 20, 30, 50 → y: 10, 14, 18, 22, 30. [3 marks — 1 for each two correct pairs after the first.]
(b) y = (2/5)(100) + 10 = 40 + 10 = 50 inches. [2 marks]
(c) Gradient = 2/5, the average growth rate in inches per year [1½]; y-intercept = 10, the current diameter of the tree in inches [1½].
(d) Any sensible real-life linear situation [1]; correct equation in the form y = mx + c [1].
Note: In graph questions, accept readings within half a small square of the stated values. Gradients must be given as fractions in simplest form unless otherwise stated.

Question 1 — Expanding brackets (B8.2.2.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) 6(x + 3) = 6x + 18. [1 mark]
(b) −5x(3x + 4) = −15x² − 20x. [2 marks — 1 for each correct term.]
(c) 3x + 12 − 2x + 10 [2]; = x + 22 [1].
(d) 12 − 10x − 6 − 6x − 12x + 4 [2]; collecting like terms: (12 − 6 + 4) + (−10 − 6 − 12)x = 10 − 28x [2].
Question 2 — Multiplication of binomials (B8.2.2.1.1)  [10 marks]
(a) a² + 3a + 2a + 6 = a² + 5a + 6. [2 marks]
(b) 4x² − 2xy + 2xy − y² [2]; = 4x² − y² [1].
(c) (2x)² + 2(2x)(3) + 3² [2]; = 4x² + 12x + 9 [1].
(d) x² + 2x − 5x − 10 [1]; = x² − 3x − 10 [1].
Question 3 — Operations on algebraic fractions (B8.2.2.1.2)  [10 marks]
(a) LCD = 6 [1]; 2(a − b)/6 + 9a/6 [1]; = (11a − 2b)/6 [1].
(b) LCD = 6 [1]; 2(2x − 1)/6 − 3(x + 3)/6 = (4x − 2 − 3x − 9)/6 [1]; = (x − 11)/6 [1].
(c) LCD = 12r [1]; 10/12r − 9/12r = 1/12r [1].
(d) (3a × 8a)/(4 × 9) = 24a²/36 [1]; = 2a²/3 [1].
Question 4 — Substitution and evaluation (B8.2.2.1.3)  [10 marks]
(a) 5(2) + 7(9) − 4(1) + 3(4) [2]; = 10 + 63 − 4 + 12 = 81 [1].
(b) 3/3 − 2/1 [2]; = 1 − 2 = −1 [1].
(c) 1/1 + 2/3 [1]; = 5/3 [1].
(d) 4 + 4 − 2(2)(−2) [1]; = 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 [1]. (Also accept recognising (x − y)² = (2 − (−2))² = 16.)
Question 5 — Factorisation (B8.2.2.1.4)  [10 marks]
(a) 3a(x + 2y). [2 marks]
(b) 27(2 − 3x). [2 marks]
(c) 25x(4 − x). [2 marks]
(d) a(x − y) − y(x − y) [1]; = (x − y)(a − y) [1].
(e) x(3x + 2y) − 4z(3x + 2y) [1]; = (3x + 2y)(x − 4z) [1].
Question 6 — Integrated algebra (B8.2.2.1.1/.4)  [10 marks]
(a) (x² + 2x − 8) − (x² − 3x) [2]; = x² + 2x − 8 − x² + 3x = 5x − 8 [1].
(b) 5(2) − 8 = 2. [2 marks]
(c) (x − 3)(x + 3). [2 marks]
(d) Any sensible two-bracket expression [1½]; correct expansion [1½].
Note: Simplified answers must collect all like terms. In factorisation, answers must be fully factorised (highest common factor taken out).

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Solving simple inequalities  [10 marks]
(a) Solve x + 3 > 5.  x > 5 − 3 → x > 2.   [2 marks]
(b) Solve −2x ≥ 6.  Divide by −2 and reverse the sign: x ≤ −3.   [2 marks]
(c) Solve 4 − 3x ≤ 10.  −3x ≤ 6 → divide by −3 (sign reverses): x ≥ −2.   [3 marks]
(d) Solve 5x + 2 < 3x + 10.  2x < 8 → x < 4.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Inequalities with fractions and brackets  [10 marks]
(a) Solve x + ½ ≥ −3/2 (curriculum exemplar).  x ≥ −3/2 − 1/2 = −2.   [2 marks]
(b) Solve −(2/3)x + 3 ≥ 3 (curriculum exemplar).  −(2/3)x ≥ 0 → multiply by −3/2 (sign reverses): x ≤ 0.   [3 marks]
(c) Solve ½(5x − 5) < x + 5.  Multiply by 2: 5x − 5 < 2x + 10 → 3x < 15 → x < 5.   [3 marks]
(d) Solve 3(x − 1) ≥ 2x + 1.  3x − 3 ≥ 2x + 1 → x ≥ 4.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Illustrating solutions on the number line  [10 marks]
Fig. 4 — Number line for your graphs.
(a) On the number line in Fig. 4, illustrate x < 5.  Open circle at 5 with an arrow/shading to the left.   [2 marks]
(b) Illustrate x ≥ −2.  Closed circle at −2 with an arrow/shading to the right.   [2 marks]
(c) Illustrate x ≤ 4.  Closed circle at 4 with an arrow/shading to the left.   [2 marks]
(d) Solve −3x − 8 > −26 and illustrate the solution on the number line (curriculum exemplar).  −3x > −18 → x < 6. Open circle at 6 with an arrow to the left.   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Reading and explaining graphs  [10 marks]
Use Figs. 1, 2 and 3 from Section A.
(a) Write the inequality shown in Fig. 1.  x > 3.   [2 marks]
(b) Write the inequality shown in Fig. 2.  x ≤ −2.   [2 marks]
(c) Write the inequality shown in Fig. 3.  x ≤ 4.   [2 marks]
(d) Explain the difference between an open circle and a closed circle on a number-line graph.  An open circle means the end value is not included (strict < or >); a closed circle means the end value is included (≤ or ≥).   [2 marks]
(e) Solve 2x − 3 ≤ 19 and illustrate the solution (curriculum exemplar).  2x ≤ 22 → x ≤ 11. Closed circle at 11 with an arrow to the left (use a number line extended to 12).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Real-life problems  [10 marks]
(a) Ama has GH₵50. She buys books at GH₵5 each and wants to keep at least GH₵20. Write an inequality for the number n of books.  50 − 5n ≥ 20.   [2 marks]
(b) Solve your inequality and state the greatest number of books Ama can buy.  5n ≤ 30 → n ≤ 6. The greatest number of books is 6.   [4 marks]
(c) A taxi charges GH₵3 per trip plus GH₵2 per kilometre. A passenger has at most GH₵23. Write and solve an inequality for the kilometres k.  3 + 2k ≤ 23 → 2k ≤ 20 → k ≤ 10. The passenger can travel at most 10 km.   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Create and solve  [10 marks]
(a) Write an inequality of your own with a variable on both sides, and solve it.  Any valid inequality correctly solved. Example: 4x + 1 < 2x + 9 → 2x < 8 → x < 4. Award 2 marks for the inequality, 2 for the correct solution.   [4 marks]
(b) Illustrate the solution of your inequality on a number line.  Correct circle type at the boundary with shading in the correct direction (for the example: open circle at 4, arrow to the left).   [3 marks]
(c) Write a real-life story that your inequality could model.  Any coherent story consistent with the inequality. Example: 'I have GH₵9 and spend GH₵4 at once plus GH₵1 per snack; I can buy fewer than 4 snacks.' Award full marks for a consistent story.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
Reference diagrams (as printed in the question paper):
Fig. 1 — angles on a straight line (not to scale).
Fig. 2 — vertically opposite angles (not to scale).
Fig. 3 — angles at a point (not to scale).
Fig. 4 — parallel lines a and b cut by a transversal (not to scale).
Fig. 5 — quadrilateral (not to scale).
Fig. 6 — exterior angle of a triangle (not to scale).
Fig. 7 — hexagon (not to scale).
Fig. 8 — similar triangles (not to scale).
1. Angle properties at a point, on a line and opposite angles  [10 marks]
Use Figs. 1, 2 and 3 from Section A.
(a) Using Fig. 1, find x and give the reason.  Angles on a straight line: x = 180° − 70° = 110°.   [2 marks]
(b) Using Fig. 2, find x and give the reason.  Vertically opposite angles: x = 65°.   [2 marks]
(c) Using Fig. 3, find x and give the reason.  Angles at a point: x = 360° − 120° − 95° = 145°.   [3 marks]
(d) Find the complement and the supplement of 35°.  Complement = 90° − 35° = 55°; supplement = 180° − 35° = 145°.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Parallel lines and a transversal  [10 marks]
Use Fig. 4 from Section A (a ∥ b).
(a) Name the pair of angles that form an 'F-shape'.  Corresponding angles.   [2 marks]
(b) Name the pair of angles that form a 'Z-shape'.  Alternate angles.   [2 marks]
(c) State the relationship between co-interior angles.  They are supplementary (add up to 180°).   [2 marks]
(d) Find x and y in Fig. 4, giving reasons.  x = 110° (corresponding angles, a ∥ b). y = 180° − 110° = 70° (co-interior angles are supplementary; equivalently y equals the alternate of the 70° at the top).   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. The polygon angle-sum formula  [10 marks]
(a) Explain why the sum of interior angles of a polygon is (n − 2) × 180°.  From one vertex, an n-sided polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles; each triangle contributes 180°, so the sum is (n − 2) × 180°. (For a quadrilateral: 2 triangles → 360°.)   [3 marks]
(b) Hence find the sum of interior angles of a pentagon.  (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°.   [2 marks]
(c) Hence find the sum of interior angles of a hexagon.  (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°.   [2 marks]
(d) A polygon has interior angles summing to 900°. How many sides has it?  (n − 2) × 180° = 900° → n − 2 = 5 → n = 7 sides.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Missing angles in figures  [10 marks]
Use Figs. 5, 6 and 7 from Section A.
(a) Find x in Fig. 5.  Quadrilateral: x = 360° − 95° − 105° − 70° = 90°.   [3 marks]
(b) Find x in Fig. 6.  Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles: 120° = 45° + x → x = 75°.   [3 marks]
(c) Find x in Fig. 7.  Hexagon sum = 720°. x + x + 130° + 110° + 120° + 140° = 720° → 2x = 220° → x = 110°.   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Similar and congruent triangles  [10 marks]
(a) Using Fig. 8, the triangles are similar. Find x.  Scale factor = 6 ÷ 3 = 2, so x = 4 × 2 = 8.   [3 marks]
(b) Two similar triangles have corresponding sides 5 cm and 15 cm. Find the side corresponding to 7 cm in the smaller triangle.  Scale factor 3 → 7 × 3 = 21 cm.   [3 marks]
(c) Explain why AAA is not a congruence condition.  AAA fixes the shape but not the size: two triangles can have equal angles yet different sizes (similar but not congruent).   [2 marks]
(d) Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 2 : 3. Find the ratio of their areas.  Areas scale as the square of the sides: 2² : 3² = 4 : 9.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Create and solve  [10 marks]
(a) Draw (freehand) a polygon of your own, label all but one of its interior angles with values of your choice, and calculate the missing angle.  Any valid polygon with a correct use of (n − 2) × 180°. Example: quadrilateral with 100°, 80°, 90° → missing = 360° − 270° = 90°. Award 2 marks for the figure/labels, 2 for the correct missing angle.   [4 marks]
(b) Write two angle facts (e.g. about parallel lines) and use them to form a short problem; solve it.  Any coherent problem using angle properties, solved correctly. Example: 'Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one angle is 115°. Find the alternate and the co-interior angles.' → 115° and 65°. Award 3 marks for a valid problem, 3 for correct answers — capped at 6.   [6 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Constructing a triangle and its inscribed circle  [10 marks]
Work with a ruler and a pair of compasses for this question.
(a) Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, ∠ABC = 60° and BC = 5 cm.  Draw AB = 6 cm; at B construct 60° and cut off BC = 5 cm; join CA (≈ 5.6 cm).   [2 marks]
(b) Bisect ∠BAC and ∠BCA, and mark the intersection of the two bisectors as I.  Correct bisector arcs for both angles; I correctly located inside the triangle.   [3 marks]
(c) Name the point I and state what meets there.  I is the INCENTRE — the point where the three angle bisectors of the triangle meet.   [2 marks]
(d) Draw the inscribed circle of the triangle and state its radius to 1 d.p.  Circle centred at I touching all three sides; radius ≈ 1.6 cm (accept 1.5–1.7 cm).   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Constructing a triangle and its circumscribed circle  [10 marks]
(a) Construct triangle PQR with PQ = 7 cm, QR = 6 cm and PR = 5 cm.  Draw PQ = 7 cm; arcs of radius 6 cm from Q and 5 cm from P meet at R; join.   [3 marks]
(b) Construct the perpendicular bisectors of PQ and QR, and mark their intersection as S.  Correct equal-radius arcs on both sides; S correctly located.   [3 marks]
(c) Name S and state its distance property.  S is the CIRCUMCENTRE — equidistant from the three vertices P, Q and R.   [2 marks]
(d) Draw the circumscribed circle and state its radius to 1 d.p.  Circle centred at S through P, Q, R; radius ≈ 3.6 cm (accept 3.5–3.7 cm).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Constructing a square  [10 marks]
(a) Construct square ABCD with AB = 6.5 cm.  Base AB = 6.5 cm; perpendiculars at A and B; arcs of 6.5 cm fix D and C; join DC.   [4 marks]
(b) Draw and measure the diagonals AC and BD, and record each to 1 d.p.  Both diagonals ≈ 9.2 cm (6.5√2 = 9.19 cm; accept 9.0–9.4 cm).   [2 marks]
(c) What angle do the diagonals of the square make where they cross?  90° — the diagonals of a square intersect at right angles.   [2 marks]
(d) State two other properties of the diagonals of a square.  They are equal in length, and they bisect each other.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Constructing a rectangle from a side and a diagonal  [10 marks]
(a) Rectangle PQRS has PQ = 6 cm and diagonal PR = 10 cm. Calculate QR.  QR = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8 cm.   [2 marks]
(b) Using these dimensions, construct the rectangle PQRS.  PQ = 6 cm; perpendiculars at Q (and P); QR = 8 cm; PS = 8 cm; join SR.   [4 marks]
(c) Draw the second diagonal QS and state its measured length.  QS = 10 cm — the diagonals of a rectangle are equal.   [2 marks]
(d) Calculate the area of the rectangle.  Area = 6 × 8 = 48 cm².   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Parallelogram and rhombus  [10 marks]
(a) Construct parallelogram ABCD with AB = 6 cm, AD = 4.5 cm and ∠DAB = 60°.  AB = 6 cm; 60° at A with AD = 4.5 cm; arcs of 6 cm from D and 4.5 cm from B fix C.   [4 marks]
(b) Measure the diagonal BD and record it to 1 d.p.  BD ≈ 5.4 cm (exact √29.25 ≈ 5.41; accept 5.2–5.6 cm).   [2 marks]
(c) State the size of ∠ABC, giving a reason.  ∠ABC = 120° — adjacent (co-interior) angles of a parallelogram are supplementary: 180° − 60°.   [2 marks]
(d) Construct a rhombus whose diagonals are 6 cm and 8 cm, and calculate its side.  Diagonals bisect at right angles: half-diagonals 3 cm and 4 cm; side = √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Equilateral triangle: inscribed and circumscribed circles  [10 marks]
(a) Construct an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm.  Base 6 cm; arcs of radius 6 cm from both endpoints meet at the apex.   [3 marks]
(b) Locate its incentre, draw the inscribed circle and state its radius to 1 d.p.  Two angle bisectors meet at the centre; circle touches all sides; r ≈ 1.7 cm (6/(2√3) ≈ 1.73; accept 1.6–1.8 cm).   [3 marks]
(c) What do you observe about the incentre and circumcentre of an equilateral triangle?  They COINCIDE — the same single point (the centre of the triangle).   [2 marks]
(d) Hence state the radius of the circumscribed circle of the triangle to 1 d.p.  R = 6/√3 ≈ 3.5 cm (accept 3.4–3.6 cm).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

JHS3_Ch13.section_b:
SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Identifying solids and drawing nets  [10 marks]
(a) State the number of faces, edges and vertices of (i) a cuboid and (ii) a triangular prism.  (i) Cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. (ii) Triangular prism: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.   [3 marks]
(b) Sketch the net of a cuboid with length 5 cm, width 3 cm and height 2 cm, and label its rectangles.  Correct cross/T-shaped net of six rectangles: two 5×3, two 5×2, two 3×2, correctly labelled.   [3 marks]
(c) How many rectangles and how many triangles are in the net of a triangular prism?  3 rectangles and 2 triangles.   [2 marks]
(d) Name the solid whose net is 2 triangles and 3 rectangles.  A triangular prism.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Deriving the cuboid surface-area formula  [10 marks]
(a) A cuboid has length l, width w and height h. When unfolded, its faces form three congruent pairs. Name the pairs and the area of each pair.  Top & bottom = lw each; front & back = lh each; two ends = wh each.   [2 marks]
(b) Hence write an expression for the total surface area.  SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh.   [3 marks]
(c) Factorise your expression.  SA = 2(lw + lh + wh).   [2 marks]
(d) Evaluate the formula for l = 7 cm, w = 5 cm, h = 3 cm.  2(35 + 21 + 15) = 2 × 71 = 142 cm².   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Cuboid surface-area problems  [10 marks]
(a) Find the total surface area of a cuboid 12 cm × 9 cm × 6 cm.  2(108 + 72 + 54) = 2 × 234 = 468 cm².   [3 marks]
(b) The cuboid is used as an open tank with no top. Find the area of its five faces.  468 − (12 × 9) = 468 − 108 = 360 cm².   [3 marks]
(c) Find the surface area of a cube of side 9 cm.  6 × 9² = 6 × 81 = 486 cm².   [2 marks]
(d) Which solid has the greater surface area, and by how much?  The cube: 486 − 468 = 18 cm² more.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Deriving the triangular-prism surface area  [10 marks]
(a) Describe the net of a triangular prism.  Two congruent triangles (the ends) and three rectangles (the lateral faces).   [2 marks]
(b) If the cross-section has area A and perimeter P, and the prism has length l, write the surface-area formula.  SA = 2A + P × l.   [3 marks]
(c) Use the formula for a right-triangle cross-section 5 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm with length 20 cm.  A = ½ × 5 × 12 = 30; P = 30; SA = 2(30) + 30 × 20 = 60 + 600 = 660 cm².   [3 marks]
(d) Explain why all three rectangles have the same length l.  Each lateral face runs the full length of the prism, so every rectangle has one side equal to l.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Triangular-prism problems  [10 marks]
(a) Find the surface area of a prism whose isosceles-triangle cross-section has base 10 cm, height 12 cm and equal sides 13 cm, with length 20 cm.  A = ½ × 10 × 12 = 60; P = 10 + 13 + 13 = 36; SA = 2(60) + 36 × 20 = 120 + 720 = 840 cm².   [4 marks]
(b) Find the lateral surface area only (the three rectangles).  P × l = 36 × 20 = 720 cm².   [3 marks]
(c) If the length is doubled to 40 cm, find the new surface area and the increase.  SA = 120 + 36 × 40 = 120 + 1440 = 1560 cm²; increase = 1560 − 840 = 720 cm².   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Applications  [10 marks]
(a) A gift carton 30 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm is wrapped without overlap. Find the area of paper needed.  2(600 + 300 + 200) = 2 × 1100 = 2 200 cm².   [3 marks]
(b) If the carton has no lid, find the paper needed.  2 200 − (30 × 20) = 2 200 − 600 = 1 600 cm².   [2 marks]
(c) A cake tin is a triangular prism with equilateral-triangle cross-section of side 8 cm (height ≈ 6.9 cm) and length 15 cm. Estimate its surface area.  2 × (½ × 8 × 6.9) + (24 × 15) = 55.2 + 360 ≈ 415.2 cm² (accept 415–416 cm²).   [3 marks]
(d) A cube of side 6 cm and a cuboid 10 cm × 6 cm × h cm have equal surface areas. Find h.  Cube SA = 216; 2(60 + 10h + 6h) = 216 → 120 + 32h = 216 → h = 96/32 = 3 cm.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Position vectors and notation  [10 marks]
(a) With O as origin, write the position vectors of M(2, 3) and N(−1, 2).  OM = (2, 3); ON = (−1, 2).   [2 marks]
(b) Find the column vector that translates A(1, 2) to B(4, 6).  AB = (4 − 1, 6 − 2) = (3, 4).   [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the magnitude of AB.  |AB| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 units.   [3 marks]
(d) Point C satisfies OC = 2 × OM. Find the coordinates of C.  OC = 2(2, 3) = (4, 6), so C(4, 6).   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Parallel vectors  [10 marks]
(a) State the condition for two column vectors to be parallel.  One is a scalar multiple of the other (a = kb), i.e. cross-multiplying gives equal products.   [2 marks]
(b) Find the values of x if the vectors (3x, 2) and (6, x) are parallel.  3x·x = 2·6 → 3x² = 12 → x² = 4 → x = 2 or x = −2.   [3 marks]
(c) Find k if (k, 6) is parallel to (2, 3).  3k = 12 → k = 4.   [2 marks]
(d) Show that (2, −3) and (−6, 9) are parallel.  (−6, 9) = −3(2, −3), a scalar multiple, so they are parallel.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Perpendicular vectors  [10 marks]
(a) State the condition for two column vectors to be perpendicular.  Their dot product is zero: ac + bd = 0.   [2 marks]
(b) Which of (−3, 4), (−3, −4), (−4, 3), (−4, −3) is perpendicular to (3, 4)?  (−4, 3): dot product = 3(−4) + 4(3) = −12 + 12 = 0.   [2 marks]
(c) Find x if (x, 4) is perpendicular to (2, −1).  2x + 4(−1) = 0 → 2x = 4 → x = 2.   [3 marks]
(d) Show that (1, 2) and (2, 1) are NOT perpendicular.  Dot product = 1(2) + 2(1) = 4 ≠ 0, so they are not perpendicular.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. The triangle law of addition  [10 marks]
(a) State the triangle law of vector addition.  AB + BC = AC (head-to-tail joining gives the resultant).   [2 marks]
(b) P(1, −3), Q(7, 5) and R(−3, 5). Express PQ, QR and PR as column vectors.  PQ = (6, 8); QR = (−10, 0); PR = (−4, 8).   [3 marks]
(c) Show that triangle PQR is isosceles.  |PQ| = √(36 + 64) = 10; |QR| = 10; two sides equal, so PQR is isosceles.   [3 marks]
(d) Verify that PQ + QR = PR.  (6, 8) + (−10, 0) = (−4, 8) = PR. ✓   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. The parallelogram law of addition  [10 marks]
(a) State the parallelogram law of vector addition.  Two vectors drawn from a common point have as resultant the diagonal of the parallelogram they determine.   [2 marks]
(b) Find the resultant of (2, 1) and (3, 4), and its magnitude to 1 d.p.  Resultant = (5, 5); |(5, 5)| = √50 ≈ 7.1 units.   [3 marks]
(c) PQRS is a parallelogram with P(x, y), Q(5, 7), R(2, 4), S(1, 3). Find x and y.  PQ = SR → (5 − x, 7 − y) = (2 − 1, 4 − 3) = (1, 1) → x = 4, y = 6.   [3 marks]
(d) Give the reason for setting PQ = SR in part (c).  Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal and parallel, so as vectors PQ = SR.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Vector journeys  [10 marks]
(a) A boat sails (3, 4) and then (−1, 2). Find the resultant displacement.  (3, 4) + (−1, 2) = (2, 6).   [2 marks]
(b) Find the magnitude of this resultant to 1 d.p.  √(4 + 36) = √40 ≈ 6.3 units.   [2 marks]
(c) Write the vector that returns the boat to its starting point.  −(2, 6) = (−2, −6).   [2 marks]
(d) A walker goes 6 km due east and then 8 km due north. Write both displacements as column vectors and find the straight-line distance from the start.  (6, 0) and (0, 8); resultant (6, 8); distance = √(36 + 64) = 10 km.   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Everyday enlargements and properties  [10 marks]
(a) Give two everyday situations that depict enlargement.  Any two valid: printing a photo at a larger size; a projector image on a screen; a shadow; a map blown up; zooming in on a phone.   [2 marks]
(b) State the two pieces of information that define an enlargement.  The centre of enlargement and the scale factor.   [2 marks]
(c) Under an enlargement, what happens to (i) the angles and (ii) the lengths of the object?  (i) Angles are unchanged. (ii) Lengths are multiplied by |k|.   [3 marks]
(d) Describe the image when the scale factor is −1.  The image is congruent to the object but on the opposite side of the centre (the object turned through 180° about the centre).   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Drawing enlargements on a grid  [10 marks]
(a) A triangle has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1) and (1, 2). Draw its image under an enlargement with centre O and scale factor 2.  Image vertices (2, 2), (6, 2), (2, 4) correctly plotted.   [3 marks]
(b) Draw the image of the same triangle under an enlargement with centre O and k = −1.  Image vertices (−1, −1), (−3, −1), (−1, −2).   [3 marks]
(c) Draw the image under an enlargement with centre O and k = ½.  Image vertices (0.5, 0.5), (1.5, 0.5), (0.5, 1).   [2 marks]
(d) State how each image compares in size with the object.  k = 2: twice as large; k = −1: same size; k = ½: half the size.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Scale factors from diagrams  [10 marks]
(a) [Fig. 1] State the scale factor and the centre of the enlargement that maps P onto Q.  k = 2, centre O(0, 0).   [3 marks]
(b) [Fig. 2] State the scale factor of the enlargement that maps P onto Q.  k = −2 (image on the opposite side, twice as large).   [2 marks]
(c) [Fig. 3] State the scale factor of the enlargement that maps P onto Q.  k = ½ (image smaller, same side).   [2 marks]
(d) Explain the effect of a negative scale factor on the position of the image.  The image lies on the opposite side of the centre from the object (inverted through the centre).   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Enlargement coordinates and areas  [10 marks]
(a) Find the image of (2, −3) under an enlargement with centre O and scale factor 4.  (8, −12).   [2 marks]
(b) Find the image of (2, 4) under an enlargement with centre (1, 1) and scale factor 3.  Vector from centre: (1, 3); ×3 = (3, 9); image = (1 + 3, 1 + 9) = (4, 10).   [3 marks]
(c) An object has area 12 cm². Find the image area when k = −2.  Area × k² = 12 × 4 = 48 cm².   [3 marks]
(d) An image has area 50 cm² and the object has area 2 cm². Find the possible values of k.  k² = 50/2 = 25 → k = 5 or k = −5.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Congruent and similar shapes  [10 marks]
(a) What are congruent shapes?  Shapes with the same shape and the same size (one fits exactly on the other).   [2 marks]
(b) What are similar shapes?  Shapes with equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides (same shape, possibly different size).   [2 marks]
(c) Two similar triangles are in the ratio 3 : 5. The smaller has perimeter 21 cm. Find the perimeter of the larger.  21 × 5/3 = 35 cm.   [3 marks]
(d) If the smaller triangle has area 18 cm², find the area of the larger.  Area ratio 9 : 25 → 18 × 25/9 = 50 cm².   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Verifying similarity  [10 marks]
(a) An object has sides 4 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm and its image has sides 12 cm, 15 cm, 18 cm. Show that the shapes are similar and state k.  12/4 = 15/5 = 18/6 = 3, all ratios equal → similar with k = 3.   [3 marks]
(b) Are the two shapes congruent? Give a reason.  No — corresponding sides are not equal (k ≠ 1), so same shape but different size.   [2 marks]
(c) If the object has area 10 cm², find the area of the image.  10 × 3² = 90 cm².   [3 marks]
(d) State the single transformation that maps the object onto the image.  An enlargement with scale factor 3 (about the centre joining corresponding vertices).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Data types and collection methods  [10 marks]
(a) Define quantitative and qualitative data, giving one example of each.  Quantitative: numerical data from counting/measuring (e.g. heights, test scores). Qualitative: descriptive, non-numerical data (e.g. favourite colour, type of food).   [3 marks]
(b) Choose and justify a method to find the most common mode of travel by learners in your school.  A questionnaire/survey — it reaches many learners quickly and gives countable (quantitative) responses that can be tallied.   [3 marks]
(c) Which method would you use to determine the lifespan of bulbs? Justify.  An experiment — the bulbs must actually be life-tested under controlled conditions; no existing records exist.   [2 marks]
(d) State one advantage of a questionnaire over an interview.  It is quicker/cheaper and can cover many respondents at once (or respondents answer privately/anonymously).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Ungrouped frequency table  [10 marks]
(a) The marks out of 10 of 20 pupils are: 4, 7, 5, 6, 4, 8, 5, 7, 6, 5, 9, 5, 5, 7, 4, 6, 8, 5, 6, 7. Construct a frequency table for the data.  Mark: 4→3; 5→6; 6→4; 7→4; 8→2; 9→1 (tallies acceptable); total 20.   [4 marks]
(b) Write down the mode.  5 (occurs 6 times).   [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the range.  9 − 4 = 5.   [2 marks]
(d) How many pupils wrote the test?  Sum of frequencies = 20.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Grouped frequency table  [10 marks]
Thirty bulbs were life-tested. Lifespans (hours): 164–167 frequency 4; 168–171 frequency 7; 172–175 frequency 11; 176–179 frequency 8.
(a) State the class width of the interval 168–171.  4 (it contains the 4 whole numbers 168, 169, 170, 171).   [2 marks]
(b) Write down the modal class.  172–175 (greatest frequency, 11).   [2 marks]
(c) Show that a total of 30 bulbs were tested.  4 + 7 + 11 + 8 = 30.   [3 marks]
(d) How many bulbs lasted 172 hours or more?  11 + 8 = 19 bulbs.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Stem-and-leaf, pictograph and pie chart  [10 marks]
(a) The ages of a club are 12, 15, 17, 20, 21, 24, 27, 32, 33. Draw a stem-and-leaf plot for the data.  Stems 1, 2, 3 with leaves: 1 | 2 5 7; 2 | 0 1 4 7; 3 | 2 3, plus a key (e.g. 2 | 4 = 24 style).   [3 marks]
(b) Use your plot to find the range of the ages.  33 − 12 = 21 years.   [2 marks]
(c) In a pictograph one symbol represents 10 books. Show how 45 books would be drawn.  Four full symbols and one half symbol (4½ × 10 = 45).   [3 marks]
(d) In a survey of 30 people, 3 chose cocoa. Find the sector angle for cocoa in a pie chart.  3/30 × 360° = 36°.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Histograms  [10 marks]
A test was marked out of 60. The marks of 30 students were grouped as follows: 10–19 frequency 4; 20–29 frequency 7; 30–39 frequency 10; 40–49 frequency 6; 50–59 frequency 3.
(a) Draw a histogram of the data.  Five touching bars on the mark axis with heights 4, 7, 10, 6, 3; correct axes labelled (marks, frequency).   [4 marks]
(b) Write down the modal class.  30–39 (frequency 10).   [2 marks]
(c) How many students wrote the test?  4 + 7 + 10 + 6 + 3 = 30.   [2 marks]
(d) Which class contains the median? Explain briefly.  The 15th and 16th values; cumulative frequencies 4, 11, 21 place both in 30–39, so the median lies in 30–39.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Create and solve  [10 marks]
(a) Create a set of seven whole numbers with mode 6 and range 5.  Any valid set, e.g. 3, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8 (mode 6 occurs 3 times; range 8 − 3 = 5).   [3 marks]
(b) Present your data in a frequency table.  Correct counts for each value used; frequencies sum to 7.   [3 marks]
(c) State the mode and the range of your data.  Mode 6; range 5 (must match the created data).   [2 marks]
(d) Pose one question that can be answered from your table, and solve it.  Any coherent question with a correct answer, e.g. 'How many 6s are there?' → 3, or 'What is the total frequency?' → 7.   [2 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Bias in data collection  [10 marks]
(a) Explain why the question 'Overall, don't you think the teaching of mathematics is very good?' is biased.  It is a leading question — the wording pushes respondents to answer 'yes' and hides their true opinion.   [2 marks]
(b) Rewrite the question without bias, including a suitable response scale.  'Overall, how will you rate the teaching of mathematics?' with scale: very poor, poor, fair, good, very good.   [3 marks]
(c) Ama surveyed only the football team about sport-related injuries. Why is this biased?  Football is a contact sport, so footballers will report more injuries than players of other sports — the sample is not representative (selection bias).   [3 marks]
(d) What should Ama do to remove the bias?  Ask more people who play a variety of sports, both contact and non-contact (athletics, tennis, volleyball, etc.).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Descriptive statistics of ungrouped data  [10 marks]
(a) The ages of 10 club members are 12, 14, 13, 15, 14, 12, 16, 14, 13, 15. Calculate the mean age.  Sum = 138; mean = 138/10 = 13.8 years.   [3 marks]
(b) Find the median age.  Sorted: 12, 12, 13, 13, 14, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16; median = (14 + 14)/2 = 14 years.   [3 marks]
(c) Write down the mode.  14 (occurs 3 times).   [2 marks]
(d) Calculate the range.  16 − 12 = 4 years.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Descriptive statistics of grouped data  [10 marks]
Bulb lifespans (hours) were grouped as 164–167, 168–171, 172–175 and 176–179.
(a) State the minimum lifespan to the nearest hour.  164 hours.   [2 marks]
(b) State the maximum lifespan to the nearest hour.  179 hours.   [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the range of the lifespans.  179 − 164 = 15 hours.   [2 marks]
(d) If the frequencies were 4, 7, 11, 8, write down the modal class.  172–175.   [2 marks]
(e) Which lifespan would you consider when ordering bulbs for your shop? Justify.  The mode/modal class (172–175) — it is the lifespan customers most often get, so it best guides stocking.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Working with the mean  [10 marks]
(a) The mean of four numbers is 6. Find their sum.  Sum = mean × n = 6 × 4 = 24.   [2 marks]
(b) Three of the numbers are 5, 7 and 4. Find the fourth.  24 − (5 + 7 + 4) = 24 − 16 = 8.   [3 marks]
(c) The mean age of 10 people is 15 years. A 26-year-old joins them. Find the new mean.  (150 + 26)/11 = 176/11 = 16 years.   [3 marks]
(d) Explain why the mean increased.  The added value (26) is greater than the old mean (15), so it pulls the mean up.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Effect of extreme data  [10 marks]
(a) For the data 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, calculate the mean, the median and the mode.  Mean = 20/5 = 4; median = 3; mode = 3.   [3 marks]
(b) The 7 is replaced by 300. Calculate the new mean.  (2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 300)/5 = 313/5 = 62.6.   [2 marks]
(c) Find the new median and the new mode. What do you notice?  Median = 3; mode = 3 — both are unchanged by the extreme value.   [3 marks]
(d) Which measure was affected most, and why?  The mean — it uses every value, so the extreme 300 pulls it from 4 to 62.6.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Interpreting with extreme values  [10 marks]
(a) Five workers earn GH₵ 900, 950, 1 000, 1 050 and the manager earns GH₵ 10 000. Calculate the mean salary.  (900 + 950 + 1 000 + 1 050 + 10 000)/5 = 13 900/5 = GH₵ 2 780.   [2 marks]
(b) Find the median salary.  GH₵ 1 000 (the middle value).   [2 marks]
(c) Which measure better represents the typical salary? Justify.  The median — four of the five salaries lie near 1 000, while the manager's extreme salary inflates the mean to 2 780, which nobody actually earns near.   [3 marks]
(d) Describe the effect of the manager's salary on the mean.  It pulls the mean far above the workers' salaries, making the mean misleading for a 'typical' pay.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Sample space and dependence  [10 marks]
(a) A bag contains 3 red, 2 green and 1 pink bottle tops. Two tops are drawn without replacement. List the possible ordered colour pairs.  RR, RG, RP, GR, GG, GP, PR, PG (PP is impossible — only one pink top).   [3 marks]
(b) Explain why the two draws are dependent events.  The first draw removes a top, changing the numbers left, so the second probability depends on the first outcome.   [2 marks]
(c) Find P(first draw is red) and express it as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.  3/6 = ½ = 0.5 = 50%.   [3 marks]
(d) Find P(pink then pink).  1/6 × 0/5 = 0 — impossible, since only one pink top exists.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Tree diagram  [10 marks]
(a) A bag has 2 blue and 3 yellow marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. Draw a probability tree diagram with fractions on the branches.  First stage B 2/5, Y 3/5; from B: B 1/4, Y 3/4; from Y: B 2/4, Y 2/4.   [4 marks]
(b) Use the tree to find P(blue then blue).  2/5 × 1/4 = 2/20 = 1/10.   [2 marks]
(c) Find P(the two marbles are different colours).  P(BY) + P(YB) = 2/5×3/4 + 3/5×2/4 = 3/10 + 3/10 = 3/5.   [2 marks]
(d) Express P(blue then blue) as a decimal and a percentage.  1/10 = 0.1 = 10%.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Card experiments (curriculum exemplars)  [10 marks]
(a) One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Find P(Ace) as a fraction.  4/52 = 1/13.   [2 marks]
(b) Two cards are drawn without replacement. Find P(two Aces).  4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221.   [3 marks]
(c) Find P(Ace then Jack) without replacement.  4/52 × 4/51 = 16/2652 = 4/663.   [3 marks]
(d) Express 1/13 as a percentage to 1 decimal place.  100/13 ≈ 7.7%.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Converting probabilities  [10 marks]
(a) Express 3/4 as a decimal and as a percentage.  0.75 and 75%.   [2 marks]
(b) Express 0.2 as a fraction and as a ratio of favourable : unfavourable.  1/5; favourable : unfavourable = 1 : 4.   [3 marks]
(c) Express 40% as a fraction in lowest terms.  40/100 = 2/5.   [2 marks]
(d) A probability of 3/5 gives which favourable : unfavourable ratio?  3 : 2 (3 favourable out of 5, so 2 unfavourable).   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Dependent draws from 4 red and 4 blue  [10 marks]
(a) Two sweets are taken without replacement. Find P(red then red).  4/8 × 3/7 = 12/56 = 3/14.   [3 marks]
(b) Find P(both sweets the same colour).  P(RR) + P(BB) = 3/14 + 3/14 = 6/14 = 3/7.   [4 marks]
(c) Hence find P(the sweets are different colours).  1 − 3/7 = 4/7.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. At least one red  [10 marks]
(a) From the 3-red, 2-green, 1-pink bag, two tops are drawn without replacement. Find P(no red).  3/6 × 2/5 = 6/30 = 1/5.   [3 marks]
(b) Hence find P(at least one red).  1 − 1/5 = 4/5.   [3 marks]
(c) Express this probability as a percentage.  4/5 = 80%.   [2 marks]
(d) Why is the complement method convenient here?  'At least one red' covers many paths (RG, RP, GR, PR, RR…); 'no red' is a single short path, so 1 − P(no red) is quicker.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

(a) Last digit = 2; first digit = 2 + 2 = 4; second digit = 3 × 2 = 6; third digit = 6 ÷ 2 = 3; fourth digit = 3 + 1 = 4; fifth digit = 6 ÷ 2 = 3. The number is 463,432. [4 marks — 1 for each of four correctly deduced digits beyond the given two, or equivalent full working.]

(a) (i) 41,237,650 ≈ 41,200,000 [2]; (ii) 4.123765 × 10⁷ [2].

Question 1 — The number system (B9.1.1.2.1)  [10 marks]
(a) {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. [2 marks]
(b) (i) −7 — rational [1]; (ii) √11 — irrational [1]; (iii) 0.375 — rational [1]; (iv) π — irrational [1].

(a) A = {1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18}; B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24}. [2 marks]
(b) A ∩ B = {1, 2, 3, 6}. [2 marks]
(c) A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24} [2]; n(A ∪ B) = 10 [1].

(b) Phone only = 70 − 15 = 55. [2 marks]

(a) Tea and coffee but not Milo = 20 − 5 = 15. [2 marks]
(b) Only Milo = 40 − 15 − 10 + 5 = 20. [3 marks]

(d) Exactly two = (12 − 5) + (8 − 5) + (10 − 5) = 15 [1]; P = 15/50 = 3/10 [1].
Check: 13 + 10 + 7 + 15 + 5 = 50. ✓

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Simplifying surds  [10 marks]
Simplify each of the following surds.
(a) √75  √75 = √(25 × 3) = √25 × √3 = 5√3   [2 marks]
(b) √48  √48 = √(16 × 3) = √16 × √3 = 4√3   [2 marks]
(c) √200  √200 = √(100 × 2) = √100 × √2 = 10√2   [2 marks]
(d) √32  √32 = √(16 × 2) = √16 × √2 = 4√2   [2 marks]
(e) √98  √98 = √(49 × 2) = √49 × √2 = 7√2   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Adding and subtracting surds  [10 marks]
Simplify each of the following, giving your answers in surd form.
(a) 5√2 + 2√2  (5 + 2)√2 = 7√2   [2 marks]
(b) 8√3 − 3√3  (8 − 3)√3 = 5√3   [2 marks]
(c) 3√5 − √5 + 2√3  (3 − 1)√5 + 2√3 = 2√5 + 2√3 (√5 and √3 are unlike surds and cannot be combined)   [2 marks]
(d) √12 + √27  √12 = 2√3 and √27 = 3√3, so 2√3 + 3√3 = 5√3   [2 marks]
(e) 10√2 − 4√2 + √2  (10 − 4 + 1)√2 = 7√2   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Multiplying and dividing surds  [10 marks]
Evaluate each of the following.
(a) √5 × √20  √(5 × 20) = √100 = 10   [2 marks]
(b) √72 ÷ √2  √(72 ÷ 2) = √36 = 6   [2 marks]
(c) 2√3 × 4√3  (2 × 4) × (√3 × √3) = 8 × 3 = 24   [2 marks]
(d) (10√6) ÷ (2√3)  (10 ÷ 2) × √(6 ÷ 3) = 5 × √2 = 5√2   [2 marks]
(e) (9√5) ÷ (3√5)  (9 ÷ 3) × (√5 ÷ √5) = 3 × 1 = 3   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Surds in context  [10 marks]
A rectangular garden has length √7 m and width √28 m.
(a) Find the area of the garden.  Area = √7 × √28 = √(7 × 28) = √196 = 14 m²   [3 marks]
(b) Simplify 4√2 + 2√2.  (4 + 2)√2 = 6√2   [2 marks]
(c) Simplify 5√2 − 2√2.  (5 − 2)√2 = 3√2   [2 marks]
(d) The garden is fenced along three sides whose lengths are √8 m, 3√2 m and √2 m. Find the total length of fencing, giving your answer in surd form.  √8 = 2√2. Total = 2√2 + 3√2 + √2 = (2 + 3 + 1)√2 = 6√2 m   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Identities and exact values  [10 marks]
(a) Evaluate √18 ÷ √2.  √(18 ÷ 2) = √9 = 3   [2 marks]
(b) Evaluate √12 × √3.  √(12 × 3) = √36 = 6   [2 marks]
(c) Evaluate (√5 + √2)(√5 − √2).  (√5)² − (√2)² = 5 − 2 = 3 (difference of two squares)   [3 marks]
(d) A square has side √5 cm. Find (i) its perimeter and (ii) its area, leaving answers in exact form.  (i) Perimeter = 4 × √5 = 4√5 cm;  (ii) Area = √5 × √5 = 5 cm²   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Create and solve  [10 marks]
(a) Write down two like surds of your own and simplify their sum.  Any correct pair of like surds with a correct simplification. Example: 2√3 and 5√3; sum = (2 + 5)√3 = 7√3. Award 1 mark for valid like surds, 2 marks for correct sum.   [3 marks]
(b) Write down two surds of your own whose product is a whole number, and evaluate the product.  Any correct pair with a whole-number product. Example: √3 and √12; product = √(3 × 12) = √36 = 6. Award 1 mark for a valid pair, 2 marks for correct product.   [3 marks]
(c) A triangle has sides √2 cm, √8 cm and √18 cm. Find its perimeter in the form a√2.  √8 = 2√2 and √18 = 3√2, so perimeter = √2 + 2√2 + 3√2 = 6√2 cm (a = 6).   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Review of fractions  [10 marks]
Answer each of the following.
(a) Write down three fractions equivalent to 2/5.  Any three of: 4/10, 6/15, 8/20, 10/25, … (multiply numerator and denominator by the same number).   [2 marks]
(b) Express 15/10 in its simplest form.  15/10 = (15 ÷ 5)/(10 ÷ 5) = 3/2.   [2 marks]
(c) Express 12/5 as a mixed number.  12 ÷ 5 = 2 remainder 2, so 12/5 = 2 2/5.   [2 marks]
(d) Express 2 5/9 as an improper fraction.  (2 × 9 + 5)/9 = 23/9.   [2 marks]
(e) Arrange 2/3, 5/8, 3/4 and 7/12 in ascending order.  Using the common denominator 24: 2/3 = 16/24, 5/8 = 15/24, 3/4 = 18/24, 7/12 = 14/24. Ascending order: 7/12, 5/8, 2/3, 3/4.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Addition and subtraction of fractions  [10 marks]
Work out each of the following, giving your answers in their simplest form.
(a) 3/4 + 7/8  6/8 + 7/8 = 13/8 = 1 5/8.   [2 marks]
(b) 1 1/2 + 4/5 − 5/6  3/2 + 4/5 − 5/6 = (45 + 24 − 25)/30 = 44/30 = 22/15 = 1 7/15.   [2 marks]
(c) 2 1/4 − 1 1/2  9/4 − 3/2 = 9/4 − 6/4 = 3/4.   [2 marks]
(d) 5/6 − 1/4 + 1/3  10/12 − 3/12 + 4/12 = 11/12.   [2 marks]
(e) 3 − 1 3/8  24/8 − 11/8 = 13/8 = 1 5/8.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Multiplication, division and BODMAS  [10 marks]
(a) Evaluate 2/3 × 3/4.  (2 × 3)/(3 × 4) = 6/12 = 1/2.   [2 marks]
(b) Evaluate 5/8 ÷ 2 1/2.  5/8 × 2/5 = 10/40 = 1/4.   [2 marks]
(c) Using BODMAS, evaluate 2/3 × 3/4 − 5/8 ÷ 2 1/2.  1/2 − (5/8 × 2/5) = 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4.   [2 marks]
(d) Using BODMAS, evaluate (3/4 + 5/8) × 4/11 − 1/2.  (11/8) × 4/11 − 1/2 = 1/2 − 1/2 = 0.   [2 marks]
(e) Using BODMAS, evaluate 3/4 ÷ 3/8 + (4/5 − 1/2).  (3/4 × 8/3) + 3/10 = 2 + 3/10 = 2 3/10.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Fractions of quantities  [10 marks]
Kofi has GH₵600. He spends 1/3 of it on school fees, 2/5 on books and saves the rest.
(a) How much does he spend on school fees?  1/3 × 600 = GH₵200.   [2 marks]
(b) How much does he spend on books?  2/5 × 600 = GH₵240.   [2 marks]
(c) What fraction of his money is left?  1 − 1/3 − 2/5 = (15 − 5 − 6)/15 = 4/15.   [3 marks]
(d) How much does he save?  4/15 × 600 = GH₵160 (or 600 − 200 − 240 = GH₵160).   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Word problems with rounding  [10 marks]
A seamstress has 25 m of cloth. She uses 3/5 of it to sew school uniforms.
(a) How many metres of cloth does she use?  3/5 × 25 = 15 m.   [2 marks]
(b) How many metres are left?  25 − 15 = 10 m.   [2 marks]
(c) She cuts the remaining cloth into pieces of 1.6 m each. How many complete pieces does she get?  10 ÷ 1.6 = 6.25, so she gets 6 complete pieces (0.25 m is left over).   [3 marks]
(d) Round 6.25 to (i) 1 decimal place, (ii) 1 significant figure.  (i) 6.3;  (ii) 6.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Create and solve  [10 marks]
(a) Write down a fraction of your own and give two fractions equivalent to it.  Any valid fraction with two correct equivalents. Example: 3/7 → 6/14 and 9/21. Award 1 mark for the fraction, 2 for correct equivalents.   [3 marks]
(b) Create a word problem that involves finding a fraction of a quantity, and solve it.  Any coherent problem solved correctly. Example: 'Find 3/4 of GH₵80' → 3/4 × 80 = GH₵60. Award 2 marks for a valid problem, 2 for the correct solution.   [4 marks]
(c) Create an expression involving addition and multiplication of fractions, and evaluate it using BODMAS.  Any valid expression evaluated correctly. Example: 1/2 + 1/3 × 3/4 = 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4. Award 1 mark for a valid expression, 2 for correct evaluation.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

1. Ratio and sharing  [10 marks]
(a) Express 36 : 48 in its simplest form.  36 : 48 = (36 ÷ 12) : (48 ÷ 12) = 3 : 4.   [2 marks]
(b) Share GH₵450 between Esi and Yaw in the ratio 2 : 3.  Total parts = 2 + 3 = 5. Esi = 2/5 × 450 = GH₵180; Yaw = 3/5 × 450 = GH₵270. Check: 180 + 270 = 450.   [4 marks]
(c) The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find each angle.  Total parts = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9; angles sum to 180°. 2/9 × 180° = 40°; 3/9 × 180° = 60°; 4/9 × 180° = 80°. Check: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180°.   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Rates and proportion  [10 marks]
(a) A bus travels 240 km in 3 hours. Find its speed.  Speed = 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h.   [2 marks]
(b) If 6 loaves of bread cost GH₵39.00, find the cost of 10 loaves.  Unit price = 39 ÷ 6 = GH₵6.50 per loaf; 10 loaves = 10 × 6.50 = GH₵65.00.   [3 marks]
Fig. 2 — GH₵250 shared between Esi and Yaw in the ratio 2 : 3
(c) Fig. 2 shows GH₵250 shared between Esi and Yaw in the ratio 2 : 3. Find each person's share.  Total parts = 5; one part = 250 ÷ 5 = GH₵50. Esi = 2 × 50 = GH₵100; Yaw = 3 × 50 = GH₵150.   [5 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Simple interest  [10 marks]
A girl deposited GH₵4,500 at the bank at a rate of 3% per annum.
(a) Write down the simple interest formula and explain each letter.  I = PRT/100, where I = interest, P = principal, R = rate per annum, T = time in years.   [2 marks]
(b) Find the simple interest earned in 3 years, and the amount.  I = (4,500 × 3 × 3)/100 = GH₵405. Amount = 4,500 + 405 = GH₵4,905.   [4 marks]
(c) What is the amount at the end of the fifth year?  I = (4,500 × 3 × 5)/100 = GH₵675. Amount = 4,500 + 675 = GH₵5,175.   [2 marks]
(d) A different investment of GH₵2,000 amounts to GH₵2,400 in 4 years at simple interest. Find the rate.  I = 2,400 − 2,000 = GH₵400. R = (I × 100)/(P × T) = (400 × 100)/(2,000 × 4) = 5%.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. VAT, discount and commission  [10 marks]
(a) A man bought an item at GH₵4,500.00, VAT inclusive at 12.5%. Calculate the basic cost and the VAT paid.  Basic cost = 4,500 ÷ 1.125 = GH₵4,000. VAT = 4,500 − 4,000 = GH₵500 (or 12.5% of 4,000).   [4 marks]
(b) A car costs GH₵80,500.00. What is its new value if there is a discount of 10%?  Discount = 80,500 × 0.10 = GH₵8,050. New value = 80,500 − 8,050 = GH₵72,450.   [3 marks]
(c) An agent's commission on the sale of a car is 3 1/2%. Calculate the commission on a car sold for GH₵68,000.00.  Commission = 3.5% of 68,000 = (3.5 × 68,000)/100 = GH₵2,380.   [3 marks]

3. Solving simultaneous equations algebraically  [10 marks]
(a) Using elimination, solve x + y = 7 and x − y = 3.  Adding: 2x = 10 → x = 5; then y = 7 − 5 = 2. Solution: (5, 2). Check: 5 + 2 = 7 ✓, 5 − 2 = 3 ✓.   [3 marks]
(b) Using elimination, solve 2x + y = 8 and x + y = 5.  Subtracting: x = 3; then y = 5 − 3 = 2. Solution: (3, 2). Check: 6 + 2 = 8 ✓, 3 + 2 = 5 ✓.   [3 marks]
(c) Using substitution, solve y = 3x and 2x + y = 15.  2x + 3x = 15 → 5x = 15 → x = 3; y = 3 × 3 = 9. Solution: (3, 9). Check: 6 + 9 = 15 ✓.   [4 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]

(a) The sum of two numbers is 10 and their difference is 4. Write two equations to represent this.  Let the numbers be x and y: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.   [2 marks]
(b) Solve your equations to find the two numbers.  Adding: 2x = 14 → x = 7; y = 10 − 7 = 3. The numbers are 7 and 3.   [3 marks]
(c) Two goats and one sheep cost GH₵700. One goat and two sheep cost GH₵800. Write equations for the cost g of a goat and s of a sheep.  2g + s = 700 and g + 2s = 800.   [2 marks]
(d) Solve the equations to find the cost of a goat and of a sheep.  Adding: 3g + 3s = 1,500 → g + s = 500. Subtracting the second original from the first: g − s = −100. So g = 200, s = 300. A goat costs GH₵200 and a sheep GH₵300.   [3 marks]

SECTION B: MARKING SCHEME
1. Change of subject  [10 marks]
(a) Make x the subject of y = 3x − 5.  y + 5 = 3x → x = (y + 5)/3.   [2 marks]
(b) Make b the subject of A = ½(a + b)h.  2A = (a + b)h → 2A/h = a + b → b = 2A/h − a.   [3 marks]
(c) Make u the subject of v² = u² + 2as.  u² = v² − 2as → u = √(v² − 2as).   [3 marks]
(d) Make l the subject of T = 2π√(l/g).  T² = 4π²(l/g) → l = gT²/(4π²).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
2. Using changed subjects with the figures  [10 marks]
Fig. 1 — Triangle with base 12 cm and height h; area 54 cm².
Fig. 2 — Cylinder with radius 7 cm and height h; volume 1,540 cm³.
(a) The area of a rectangle is 24 cm² and its length is 8 cm. Find the width (curriculum exemplar).  b = A/l = 24/8 = 3 cm.   [2 marks]
(b) A circle has an area of 154 cm². Taking π = 22/7, find its radius (curriculum exemplar).  r² = A ÷ π = 154 × 7/22 = 49 → r = 7 cm.   [3 marks]
(c) Using Fig. 1, the triangle has an area of 54 cm². Find h (curriculum exemplar).  h = 2A/b = (2 × 54)/12 = 108/12 = 9 cm.   [2 marks]
(d) Using Fig. 2, the cylinder has a volume of 1,540 cm³. Taking π = 22/7, find h.  h = V ÷ πr² = 1,540 ÷ (22/7 × 49) = 1,540 ÷ 154 = 10 cm.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
3. Substitution  [10 marks]
(a) Find the value of (x − b)² − 3(x − b) when x = 2 and b = −5 (curriculum exemplar).  x − b = 2 − (−5) = 7; so 7² − 3 × 7 = 49 − 21 = 28.   [3 marks]
(b) Evaluate 3p² − 2pq + q² when p = 2 and q = −1.  3 × 4 − 2 × 2 × (−1) + 1 = 12 + 4 + 1 = 17.   [3 marks]
(c) The volume of a cone is ⅓πr²h. Find the volume when r = 7, h = 21 and π = 22/7 (curriculum exemplar).  ⅓ × 22/7 × 49 × 21 = 22 × 7 × 7 = 1,078 cm³.   [2 marks]
(d) Using v = u + at, find v when u = 5, a = 2 and t = 4.  v = 5 + 2 × 4 = 13.   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
4. Factorisation (curriculum exemplars)  [10 marks]
Factorise each expression.
(a) 3x + 4xy  x(3 + 4y).   [2 marks]
(b) 12ab + 16b  4b(3a + 4).   [2 marks]
(c) −13xy + 39x  −13x(y − 3).   [2 marks]
(d) 8y − 2y²  2y(4 − y).   [2 marks]
(e) ax + ay + bx + by  a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (a + b)(x + y).   [2 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
5. Mixed: substitution and factorisation  [10 marks]
(a) Make h the subject of E = mgh.  h = E/(mg).   [2 marks]
(b) Hence find h when E = 500, m = 2 and g = 10.  h = 500/(2 × 10) = 25.   [2 marks]
(c) Factorise completely 4x² − 16.  4(x² − 4) = 4(x + 2)(x − 2).   [3 marks]
(d) Hence solve 4x² − 16 = 0.  4(x + 2)(x − 2) = 0 → x = −2 or x = 2.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
6. Create and solve  [10 marks]
(a) Write a formula from a real-life situation of your own, then change its subject to a different letter.  Any valid formula correctly transposed. Example: cost C = 5n for n items; making n the subject gives n = C/5. Award 2 marks for the formula, 2 for the correct transposition.   [4 marks]
(b) Write an algebraic expression of your own and factorise it completely.  Any factorisable expression correctly factorised. Example: 9x + 6x² = 3x(3 + 2x). Award 1 mark for the expression, 2 for correct factorisation.   [3 marks]
(c) Substitute values of your own into your expression from (b) and evaluate it.  Correct substitution and evaluation. Example: at x = 2: 9(2) + 6(4) = 18 + 24 = 42. Award 1 mark for substitution, 2 for the correct value.   [3 marks]
    [Total: 10 marks]
